speechtext: Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 137, to amend the Militia Act.

Explain.
Major-General MEWBURN: One of the amendments is in connection with section 24, of the Militia Act, which provides that there shall continue to be a permanent force which shall consist of sudh permanently embodied corps, not exceeding 5,000 men, enrolled for continuous service, as are from time to time authorized by the Governor in Council. It is proposed to substitute " 10,000 " for " 5,000," so as to provide that the permanent force shall consist of such permanently embodied corps not exceeding 10,000, as are from time to time authorized by the Governor in Council.
Another amendment is in connection with section 53 and 54. Section 53, subsection 2, provides that the Governor in Council may
from time to time fix the sum to be paid to privates in the permanent corps, having regard to length of service, good conduct and efficiency. It is proposed that the following words be struck out:
but the ordinary pay shall not exceed the amounts following, that is to say;	,
For privates, per diem, 75 cents.
For buglers under 18 years of age. r-er diem,
40 cents.
Section 54 of the Militia Act reads:
When on active service, during the period of annual drill and training, and when otherwise on duty, the pay and allowances of officers and men of the Active Militia, other than the Permanent Force, shall be,
(a)	for officers, warrant officers and noncommissioned officers, such rates as may be prescribed ;
(b)	for privates, at the rate of 50 cents per
diem, which rate may be increased, as prescribed, up to a maximum of one dollar per diem:	*
(c)	an allowance of a dollar per diem, or such other rate as is prescribed, to each officer and man for every horse actually and necessarily used by him.
It is proposed, by striking out subsections (a), (b) and (c) and substituting the words " at such rates as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council " to leave to the Governor in Council the fixing of the pay for active militia that may be called out for active service.

Consideration of a message from the Senate, further amending toy a consequential amendment an amendment made by the House of Commons and disagreeing to certain amendments made by the House of Commons to Bill No. 19, from the Senate, to consolidate and amend The Railway Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The amendments which have been sent to this House from the Senate relate to a very important Bill, and we all realize how desirable it is that a conclusion should be reached which would permit that Bill to become law at the present session. As to the consequential amendment proposed by the Senate 1 do not see any objection. It is merely a provision that the annual sum of $200,000 which is provided by Parliament for the purpose of ensuring the public safety should be expended subject to the provisions of the Act as amended. The other amendments are more serious, and therefore, I move:
That the consequential amendment made toy the Senate to clause 262 of Bill No. 19 letter A of the .Senate, an Act to amend! and consolidate the Railway Act, be agreed to; and that a message be sent to the Senate respectfully requesting a free conference with their Honours to consider the said Bill and any amendment which at such conference it may be considered desirable to make thereto.

Before that motion is put, may I be permitted to ask the Prime Minister if interested parties will be given an opportunity to attend this conference and be heard before the committee? I am particularly interested in section 325, which

was put through this House, I submit without proper consideration. Personally, I should like to have an opportunity of expressing the views of my constituents as to that amendment. I did not have that opportunity on the third reading, although it had been agreed that I should be enabled to speak on the subject then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was some misunderstanding as to the date at which the third reading of this Bill should be moved. I expected that my hon. friend (Mr. McQuarrie) would have put forward his views on the third reading, but he was under the impression that the Bill was not to be taken up jmtil another day. Of course, I regret the misunderstanding. Indeed, had I known that the hon. member was under a misapprehension, I should have had him notified as to the third reading. A free conference between this House and the Senate is brought about by the appointment of managers by this House and by the Senate, and it is not according to precedent as I understand, that 'the joint conference between the two Houses should listen to arguments by delegations or by members other than the managers themselves. I have had several telegrams from different parts of 'the country desiring that very considerable time should be devoted to the hearing of arguments by various interests concerned in this Bill. I have replied in the sense in which I am now replying to my hon. friend. I do not think it would be possible to carry out a conference in the way in which the constitutional practice dictates if time were occupied in listening to arguments which should properly be made before the Railway Committee, or in the House of Commons or in the Senate. If my hon. friend desires to make any representations to the conference and if he will be good enough to submit them to me I shall endeavour to see that they are received by the conference. But I do not think I can promise him anything more than that.

The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment of Mr. McMaster thereto (resumed from Friday, June 13.)

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to vote

against this amendment and, when the time comes, to vote for the motion, I do not believe that any useful purpose can be served by equivocation. In circumstances such as those with which we are faced at the present tame, it behooves us all to be as precise as we can in our views on the questions involved in this debate; for, at all events, our constituents will require from us such an attitude. I do not propose to enter into any academic discussion of the relative merits of free trade and protection, because I think it would be unnecessary and would result in no particular benefit. It would rather help matters in considering the situa-ation that exists to-day, if I were to endeavour to ascertain if possible just where we stand on the great questions that confront us, and also to discuss the reasons which should impel and shape any action we may take in the premises. For my part, I confess frankly that I have no apologies to offer and no excuses to make for any step I may take. I believe that the course I am about to follow is right as being in the interests of the people whom I represent, and in accord with the understanding that exists between us. Convinced of the rightness of my views, I have come to the conclusion which will dictate my course.
Now, a very substantial reduction has been made in the tariff. That, I think, is generally conceded in this House, and the question I ask is: How has it come about that the Government undertook to make a reduction at all? Under the system of government which we have, the responsibility rests with the people, to decide, by the course they take at general elections and through the votes of their representatives in Parliament, what the fiscal policy of the country shall be; and if I remember correctly, the last mandate of the people of Canada was given in the year 1911, when the question of reciprocity with the United States was fought out and determined. At that time the people declared against reciprocity, and the Conservative Government came into power on the outcome of that issue. That was the last instruction from the people on the tariff question, because I care not what any one may say to the contrary, tariff matters did not constitute the principal topic at the last election two years ago Conscription was then the leading issue, and, therefore, I repeat that the people of Canada, in their last mandate to their representatives in Parliament emphatically declared against the reciprocity treaty, which embodied reductions in the tariff. At the same time, I wish

to say that the constituency which I represent just as emphatically declared in favour of the reciprocity agreement, and 1 know that particularly because I was the victim on that occasion and was roundly trounced to the extent of over a thousand votes. The reciprocity treaty has now been recognized by the Government in their tariff proposals, and in fact they have gone further, if we take cognizance of the Orders in Council which were passed covering tractors and other farm implements. Speaking for my constituency, therefore, I will say that the Government has now enabled me to satisfy in this respect the desire of the people whom I represent. I asked a moment ago how it came about that the Government had made reductions in the tariff. To answer this question it is necessary that I should mention a few facts. The other day I happened to be on the train and picked up a newspaper which contained a paragraph that struck me as being very significant indeed. It appeared in the Montreal Star of June 6, the day after the Budget speech was delivered, if I remember correctly. The article reads:
Through all the preliminary discussion, however, the particular subject of speculation has been over the Western members. But for them probably no changes would have been madie at all. Throughout the session they have been holding caucuses and urging on the Government to do something " substantial."
I think that is absolutely correct. I believe that the changes which have been made in the tariff have been made entirely because of the agitation which has been carried on by the West. We have had, for the first time, I fancy, in the history of Parliament, a western caucus and in that we have been united. Old time Liberals united with old time Conservatives on the one point that they should try to get substantial reductions in the tariff, because the tariff, as it exists to-day, and as it existed for a number of years, has borne with undue weight on the people of the western provinces. I have enjoyed very much the western caucuses and I have felt that the credit due to the western members in attendance at those caucuses comes to all alike. I do not think that any one of them can be singled out as deserving of any greater credit than any other unless possibly it be the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) who, persistently, but in his own judicious way, has appealed to the judgment and sense of fair play of every one with whom he came in contact with regard to this question. We have founded our claims upon justice. If there
is an injustice being done to any section of the community, I believe that, if we appea' to the people of Canada to remove that injustice, they will do so.
I am one of those who believe that independence within the party is really the most effective kind of independence. For a number of years in Western Canada it has been my privilege to take a more or less active part in politics and on many occasions I have had the pleasure of meeting in debate the premier of Saskatchewan, the Hon. Walter Scott, a recognized leader in the Liberal party, and his view always was that the most effective sort of independence was independence within the party itself. 1 am convinced that independence on the part of western members has secured a larger measure of tariff reduction than has ever before been found possible since Parliament assembled. Such being the case, and believing, as I do, as a Conservative, who has always supported Protection, that the tariff is bearing with undue weight on Western Canada, that we should further continue our efforts and not being entirely satisfied with the reductions which have been made, I consider it my duty to remain here and to continue that independence within the party which has characterized my course in the past, the exercise of which on the part of Western members has largely produced the success that we have had already, and which will bring the additional successes that I am sure are to come.
I do not know that I am altogether satisfied with the strategy that has been employed by some of the leaders of those who are demanding a reduction of the tariff in Western Canada. To me, it would' seem a proper question to ask: Is this a war year? We cannot get away from that argument. The hon. member, for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), the first lieutenant of the leader of the Opposition, concurred in the view that this is still a war year and that we must deal with the questions with which we are confronted on that basis. I think we should have confined ourselves largely to war problems, to have held off till these problems are met, to have' dealt with our returned soldiers first and to have asked the farmers to lay aside their demands for changes until we had solved the problems of the returned soldiers, and to turn in and help us to solve those problems. 1 feel satisfied that the farmers would have done that if they had been asked, because I know, at all events in the constituency

which I have the honour to represent, the farmers have given of their sons as plentifully as any other part of the community. Therefore, they are directly interested in effecting that final settlement for our returned boys which is so necessary. Had that programme been followed, I am satisfied that a large element amongst the returned men would have rallied to the support of the farmers, something we cannot expect now as fully as if we had given them the right of way to which they are entitled.
Substantial reductions have been made in the tariff. What do they amount to? The hon. the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) stated that they amounted to $17,000,000. Is that all that is coming to the credit of the Western members? If it be true that the Western members, by their continuous agitation, have succeeded in effecting that reduction, is that all that is to be included in it? I am not a free trader. I have never yet been able to accept in its entirety the reasoning in support of free trade. I have never heard a man yet discussing free trade who would admit that the actual tariff indicated the actual tax levied on the community; that if there is a tariff tax of $17,000,000 that goes into the treasury there is an equal amount that is paid into the pockets of the manufacturers. Since I came down this session I have heard in caucus, in committee rooms and in conversation the statement made especially by those who believe in free trade, that under the tariff double the amount is paid to the manufacturer that actually goes into the treasury of the country. If that tax is levied as the result of the tariff is it not equally true that that amount which does not go into the treasury is also reduced by reason of the reductions which have been made? I am not going to press the argument, but I would like somebody to tell me, if that he true, what becomes of this additional amount when the tariff is reduced?
There is another thing that is lost sight of by those who are inclined to think, or those who are trying to tell us-especially the press-that the reductions are not as great as they should have been. I would like to have seen more and 'I expect to stay here until we see more-make no mistake about that-but if it is true that the Western members have succeeded in effecting this reduction-this saving-of $17,000,000 in taxation, then it is equally true that when we forced that reduction we compelled the Finance Minister to provide in some other way the equivalent of the taxes 
that will no longer be paid into the treasury. The Finance Minister undertook to balance up the accounts by putting .an additional tax upon the wealthier part of the community. That is what the people of this country have long been wanting. By the course that we have pursued we have not only brought about a saving of $17,000,000 in actual taxes, but we have .compelled the Finance Minister to add $17,000,000 to the taxes of those who are well able to pay them. Looking at it in that way, we are entitled to credit for an amelioration of the burdens of the people of the West to the extent of $34,000,000 through the course which we have pursued since we came down here. Is that worth taking credit for? I think it is. The fact that we have succeeded thus far as well as we have indicates to my mind the advisability of continuing in the line that we have been pursuing until we succeed in entirely eliminating the unjust burdens which bear so heavily on the people of Western Canada.
But we have an amendment. To me it is rather strange that it should have been moved by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I am sorry that the hon member is not in his seat to-day, but that is not my fault. I do not think this amendment looks like the hon. member for Brome at all. I know, Mr. Speaker, that I am not supposed to refer to a former debate which has taken place during the present session, but I can recall another resolution which the hon. gentleman moved not so very long ago. It is a very different resolution from that which is now before us-at least it seemed to me that it was. That resolution was very frank, very candid, and very specific; it stated exactly what the hon. gentleman wanted and what he proposed to do. As for the present amendment, I cannot see that there is anything candid or frank about it, or that there is anything specific or definite in its terms. I do not know where it leads to, and I am satisfied that the mover of the amendment himself does not know either.
The last clause of the amendment states:
Also, the reciprocal offer of trade with the United'.States should be accepted.
As I understand it, the reciprocal arrangement has practically been accepted by the Budget which has been brought down. With the substantial reductions that were previously made, we are now securing more for our section of the country than could have been secured under the reciprocity agreement referred to; and so far as that part of

the amendment is concerned, we do not need to waste very much time upon it.
In another clause of the amendment it is proposed:
To take off or substantially reduce as may be expedient and just to all interested.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, it is proposed to be expedient first, and to be just afterwards; justice must follow expediency. Evidently that is the idea of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster). For my part, I would put it the other way around. At any rate, the hon. gentleman proposes:
To take off, or substantially reduce, as speedily as may be expedient and just to all interested, the duties upon all other necessaries of life.
Now who is included in that? Well, that takes in everybody in the Dominion. Sir Joseph Flavelle could find plenty of room to come in under the terms of that proposition. He and all his herd of-what shall I term them-bacon hogs, could get in under the terms of that proposition without any trouble at all. More than that, Sir, you could take all the implement manufacturers of Canada and bring them within the terms of that clause of the amendment-you cculd find plenty of room there for all of them. I also believe you could bring the real simon-pure unadulterated free-trader in this House, the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) under that clause of the amendment. He could find a place under it. because it includes everybody, it does not seem to lead anywhere. As 1 understand the matter the grain growers in cur part of the country have always objected to just such amendments as this because they say "the big interests" as they term them of the East do not come into the open, they never discuss anything in the open; they go slyly to the leaders of the Government and they whisper in their ear what they want, and as a result of that they get just about what they are asking for. I am not saying this is done, but there is a very general impression in our part of the country that that is the procedure followed. The amendment uses the phraseology "when it is expedient." May I ask when it will be expedient to take the course proposed? As the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) said the other night, "expedient" may mean any time. It may be ten years or a hundred years from now-there is no saying when it might be. If it is left to hon. gentlemen opposite to say they could make any arrangement they saw fit with any party they cared to enter into an arrangement with. We have in this House, Sir, a situation something like this: We
have a party which professes, on occasions at least, to be a free-trade party and the leader of that party in this House said not very long ago that he is a protectionist. What, therefore, may we expect? We on this side feel, if we take this amendment as it has been framed, that we will get just what we got in years gone by-promises and nothing but promises; and when it comes down to tariff reductions we will not get any reductions at all. For my part I prefer very much to deal with a body of men such as the present Government-a government which has listened to the voice of the West and has gone as far as they could go for the time being in the matter of the reductions for which we have been asking, following that up with a promise that in a very short time they will have an inquiry made and in due course will make a complete revision of the tariff which will undoubtedly result in the removing of those burdens of which we complain in the West. I want to say that when I find a government dealing honestly with us, as the present Government have done- listening to us, as they have listened, during the whole session, taking the reasons which they have given and applying them to the conditions that exist to-day, and giving us the result which they have given, I must say that they have furnished me with ground upon which I can vote for them in the expectation of getting further action in the same direction. It looks to me at least that they are trying to be sincere and honest with us in our effort to solve these problems which we undoubtedly have before us. Moreover, it seems to me that the Government's method of " balancing up " as between the rich and the poor is the greatest financing that was ever carried out in Canada. They have removed $17,000,000 of taxation from the poorer classes of this country. They have increased the income tax and continued the excess profits tax for another year. As nearly as I can figure it out there will accrue to the Treasury from these, between $40,000,000 and $50,000,000. That, I maintain, is the most substantial " balancing up " as between the rich and the poor in Canada that has ever been carried out by any government in Canada.
Under those circumstances, believing as I do that the farmers and the workingmen of our country should have a chance to live, I think it would be criminal on my part to take the reins of office from the present Government and hand them over to a body of men who will submit such an amendment that I cannot understand and which

apparently is not understood by the mover and the rest of the gentlemen supporting it. Mr. Speaker, it looks to me very much like what happens around my house every fall. When the fly season, gets very bad my good wife places a small quantity of sugar and some vinegar into a saucer with a little bit of strychnine. When the concoction is thoroughly mixed and resorted to, the -strychnine is most effective in its results. But in this case I do not wish to take any chance of anything of that kind.
What can I do in a situation such as this? As I have already said, there are still problems in Western Canada that are unsolved, there are further reductions in the tariff to be made which I intend to shortly specify. Suppose I was not satisfied with the Government's action and made up my mind to change over, what would happen? Could I go over to the Opposition as it is constituted to-day? Would it be possible for me to enter their company, after their actions of this session, and then go back to my part of the country and express satisfaction with what I had done? The actions of hon. gentlemen opposite this session have shown that they are not in any way sympathetic towards the demands of the people of Western Canada. As you know, Mr. Speaker-at least you ought to know because I think you have been following events pretty closely- the people of the West have been, and still are, thoroughly in favour of the nationalization of our railroads-they are practically unanimous on that point. Were the Opposition in favour of that policy when it was submitted to the (House? There is no question at all but that they voted against the public ownership of l-ailroads. Again, when it came to building branch lines in Western Canada, what attitude did they take? You know, as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, they kept us here night after night while they talked in opposition to the plans of the Government, trying to thwart us in our effort to get branch lines constructed out there. Can I associate myself politically with those gentlemen and then go back to that part of the country and explain why I did it? It is utterly impossible. I would like somebody who could explain this amendment, because it is unexplainable to me, to go out with me into the southern part of the province of Saskatchewan, where they have no railroads, where they have no branch lines, and ask them to swallow the amendment and do without the branch railw-ays which they need and for which they have been waiting for twenty

or thirty years. I know which of the two things the people out there would prefer. I know what the people out there, w-hen it comes to the point, are going to take. Th.ey are practical people; they want results. They do not want any such nonsensical resolution, such as this, containing nothing.
But. Sir, if I did not want to go over to the Opposition benches where could I go? I understand they have established some cross benches in this House. Would it be possible for me to find a place on those benches beside my smiling friend, the free trade member for Red Deer? I think we would adorn those benches-although so far as adornment is concerned I am going to give you a little personal incident. I have a daughter and she comes here pretty regularly. I asked her the other night if she thought I should go and sit on the cross benches. She said she did not know. I said that I would like to have a photograph of myself showing what I would look like. She said, "I have a camera all right, but I have looked all over Ottawa and cannot find an owl on a hen roost." Over there I would look wise, but what could I accomplish? What would be the result? There is a little body of men out in our part of the country that would do anything to defeat Union Government, because they want the old patronage system back as quickly as possible. If I went over to the cross benches they would cheer, and I would be a little god in their eyes. I would be a power at home, but absolutely impotent at Ottawa.
In my view these cross benches have no place in our parliamentary system. You can have fifteen third parties if you want to, but at the present juncture you can accomplish nothing from those cross benches. What is the use if you can accomplish nothing, if you are merely impotent? When I come to that stage I want to be taken out of the House. If I cannot accomplish something, let me go home and stay there. I prefer to stay where I am. We Western members have shown that we have succeeded in accomplishing something for the people of Western Canada.
But rwould it be possible for me for another reason to go over to the cross benches? The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has taken his position there. Personally I think he is one of the finest members I ever met. But while I admire him, I do not approve of his deserting his post at a time when duty called him pretty strongly. (I do not intend to desert my post; I purpose to stay until my duty

is performed. But my hon. friend has gone over to the cross benches, and undoubtedly if others follow him a third party might be formed of which he would be the leader. Can I, in view of the situation that is now facing Saskatchewan, consistently follow him? Would it be possible?
Let me draw the attention of the House to this fact, that we have in the province of Saskatchewan what is known as a farmers' Parliament. It is about ten times larger, numerically speaking, than this Parliament. Usually between two and three thousand of their delegates meet every year to discuss questions relating to the farm. Last winteT they came to my own city and they could not find any place big enough for their meetings. The one thing they were absolutely unanimous in regard to was that the Government of Canada should fix the price of wheat, and I entered into an agreement with them that if I came down here I would support that policy, because I believed it to be a good policy. Has it been carried out? Most decidedly not. On Friday night the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) placed the blame for that upon the Finance Minister. I may be wrong, but I cannot for the life of me see how- the Finance Minister could be blamed. If under our system of responsible Government responsibility for matters pertaining to any particular department does not rest upon the minister of that department, then I do not understand responsible government at all. It seems to me that the responsibility for dealing with all matters concerning agriculture rests upon the Minister of Agriculture, and it was up to the Minister of Agriculture to deal with that question. Had the Finance Minister undertaken to interfere, I fancy that the Minister of Agriculture would have had good cause to immediately hand in his resignation.
But what happened? We came down to this House and went into the Agricultural Committee, which is so splendidly presided over by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders). In that committee one day, very much to my surprise, the Minister ol Agriculture announced that it was his personal opinion that the price of wheat should not be fixed. I asked him whether or not the Government had so decided, and he replied that it was his own personal opinion. I advised him to be 4 p.m. very careful because his statement would be spread broadcast throughout Canada the next day. The next day it was known all over' Canada that the Government had decided to refuse to fix
the price of wheat, and that that course was taken by reason of the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture. The farmers' parliament unanimously passed a resolution calling upon the Minister of Agriculture and the Government to fix the price of wheat. Notwithstanding that we find the Minister of Agricuture sticks his knife into the proposal and refuses to be governed by the Farmers' Parliament of Saskatchewan.
As the representative of a Saskatchewan constituency can I unite myself with my hon. friend after he has thrown down the Farmers' Parliament of Saskatchewan? Can I go back to my constituents and say, that notwithstanding that this new leader of ours has stuck his knife right up to the hilt into your proposal, I aon going to ally myself with him? I cannot do it. And I want to point out to the members from Saskatchewan that that is a vital point when they come to deal with the farmers of that particular province. As I have already said, I do hot intend to desert my post of duty after having succeeded as we western members have. Having found it utterly impossible to go anywhere else, I have come to the conclusion that the only thing to do is to stay where I am,-to stay not only with the Government as it is to-day, but- to stay with the western caucus. We may have to eliminate a couple of members-I hope not, I hope they will all come in-but through that western caucus we can accomplish a great deal, as we have already demonstrated, and my advice to hon. members from Saskatchewan is that they stick together like a bunch of western burs, and so succeed in getting in the future even more than we have got in the past.
They can have all the cheers and all the glory and .honour they want, but for my part I would very much prefer to go back to my constituents shortly after this next inquiry is made with another 7i per cent reduction in the tariff, for I think the people out there will be much more satisfied with that; they want results. It seems to me that the inquiry promised by the Government is the proper course to pursue. If we undertook to revise the tariff at the present time, the revision could not help but carry with it a war-time flavour, which would undoubtedly mean that the revision would result in a higher tariff than if made under normal conditions.
If we made a general revision to-day, what would be the result. We would not have another one for probably seven or eight years, and the farmers and working men -would have to carry the burden of the

higher tariff for those seven or eight years. Whereas by accepting the arrangement made now to proceed with an inquiry, we would have a much more satisfactory tariff than we could possibly have at the present time. We might lose a year, but as against that we would gain seven or eight years, and achieve much greater results.
I wish .to say to the Minister of Finance that I for one .propose to hold him closely to the undertaking which he has made immediately to institute an inquiry into conditions affecting the tariff and that a general revision of ithe tariff will be undertaken. I know that he means what he says. I have had a good deal to do with the Minister of Finance since I first became acquainted with him about a year ago, and I must say that I have been very much impressed by his sincerity; he has not made a single promise which he has not carried out. I have no reason, therefore, to doubt that he will carry out the inquiry which he has promised. I wish, however, to give him one or two reasons why the inquiry should be made and to cite one or two instances of the manner in which people of Western Canada have suffered.
Some of our troubles out there are due to the tariff. It is, unfortunately, a habit of some people, to blame everything upon the tariff. That is a bad policy to pursue, because those who do so are not making a proper diagnosis of the case and are certainly not giving proper treatment; and the result is that the ill is not cured at all. Some of the things, I say, that we are suffering from out there are not due to the tariff. Our geographical position is very much against us in Saskatchewan, no matter from where we get our goods. If we bring them from British Columbia, we have a high freight rate, situated as we are in the centre of the country; if we bring them from the East, the same applies. When we bring our goods from the North we are also met with the impossible, and when we go to the South we are met with the tariff. Our people, being surrounded with the impossible, as it were, naturally follow the usual course; they take the line of least resistance, try to secure a removal of the tariff.
Let us take the item of dried fruits. I know that dried fruits are used all over Canada, but I am giving this only as one example; I could cite a dozen-yes, twenty -such cases if time would permit. Dried fruits are much more important to Saskatchewan than they are to any other part of the country. In British Columbia

they have fresh fruits, and they do not have to depend upon the importation of dried fruits; and the same may be said of Ontario and of the Maritime Provinces. But we have to import this commodity, mostly from California. I wish to quote here an extract from a letter from a firm of wholesale grocers in Western Canada, one of the largest firms out there, which will indicate to you what the conditions are in that regard. If we consume more dried fruits than are consumed in other provinces, and if there is a high duty upon them, it stands to reason that we in 'Saskatchewan are paying a larger proportion of the duty than is paid by the other provinces of Canada. That is exactly what the situation is. The letter to which I have referred deals with a number of things; I will quote only that part of it which refers to the question of peaches. It reads:-
We used to buy peaches regularly at 5 and 6 cents per pound, and the price now is 15 and 16 cents per pound.
These people are not big interests at all; they are arguing for a reduction of the tariff in the interests of the common people.
You can see, when you add the heavy duties to this what it does to the price.
The duty upon the dried fruits is on an ad valorem basis. The original selling price in the country from which they are imported has increased since 1914 by 300 per cent. You cannot by any means blame the Canadian tariff for that. A free trader like the member for Bed Deer ('Mr. Michael Clark) might say that the tariff of United States was responsible for that. That may be; I am not going to argue that point. But the fact is that the price of that particular article increased in United States by 300 per cent, before it reached the Canadian boundary line at all; therefore, up to that point the tariff is not concerned. This is not a question of the protection of manufacturers within Canada; it is a question of the price of foodstuffs, and it involves a burden which bears heavily upon us in the West. But what is the result of the increase of 300 per cent in the market value of these goods in the country from which they are imported? Section 40 of the Customs Act reads:-
Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value fo-r duty shall he the fair market value thereof, when sold for home consumption, in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time when the same were exported directly to Canada.
This duty is an ad valorem one, and if this statutory provision is carried out-and

I fancy it is, because the customs authorities do not let many people escape-then the duty upon that class of goods has been increased by 300 per cent., which means that we are to-day collecting on that particular article a far higher rate of duty and a much higher tax than was intended when the tariff was levied. It may be that in another year or two the price will come back to 5 or 6 cents a .pound, in which case the duty also would fall; but in the meantime, we are faced with this severe tax upon one of our important articles of food. You can see, therefore, why, under such circumstances, there is a great deal of discontent in that country.
I could give many instances of this kind, but I shall not refer to them at length. 1 wish, however,, to direct the attention of the Finance Minister to one or two cases in order to show that it is not only the workingmen and the farmers who suffer from the conditions which I have described, and to emphasize my contention that the inquiry proposed by the minister should be carried out as speedily as conditions will permit and a revision of the tariff made with a view to overcoming these difficulties.
Some four or five years ago a large company built a plant in Regina at a cost of 13,000,000. They imported their fabricated steel from United States, paying a duty upon it of 30 per cent. That was all right; they made no complaint about that. The plant is in operation now. Another American company, finding that the company which had been previously established was taking the Canadian trade away from them, came to the conclusion that it was necessary that they also should establish a plant in Regina in order to hold their business. So they secured a property in Regina and have started to put up a plant. But in the meantime the fabricated steel which they also must import, has increased in value by one hundred per cent, and under the Customs regulations which I have read, the duty is just so much increased over that paid by theii competitors four years ago. In other words, the company established four years ago paid a duty of thirty per cent on their fabricated steel, while the new company must pay a duty of sixty per cent. That is unfair, and prevents competition. It means that this new company must have a much higher capitalization than it would otherwise have, and as it must pay interest on that capitalization it is not in a position to engage in competition that it otherwise would engage
in. The principle is the same as that which was applied by hon. gentlemen opposite in 1907 when they undertook to reduce the tariff on certain agricultural implements and then increased the valuation for duty purposes, upon which they collected that tariff. The only difference is that to-day the principle is worked out not through an action of the Government, but because of war conditions. I hope that, by reason of these illustrations, the minister will understand as strongly as I do th&t this inquiry should be proceeded with and completed as quickly as possible, and a revision made at the earliest day so that the inequalities to which I have referred may be removed.
I now come to another phase of this subject. The firm of wholesale grocers whose letter I read, have been giving me a good deal of information in another line. I shall not blame the Government for the case to which I am about to refer; I blame the Senate, because they did something recently which I do not think they had any good reason for doing. Last session the House of Commons passed an Act which the Senate rejected; I understand that the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce is trying to put that legislation through again this session. I refer to the measure with respect to canned goods, goods in packages, etc. I quote from a letter which I-hold in my hand:
I am taking- jam as a typical instance of the present situation, it is supposed to be sold in a four-pound tin, some manufacturers put it up four pounds gross, and others four pounds net so that there is a difference between four to six ounces in the actual net weight of the jam
between different manufacturers	In
the first place the consumer would be certain that when he bought four pound pails of jam that he was getting four pounds of jam and not three three-quarters pounds or less.
When I got this, I knew what conditions were in the West, but I made up my mind that I was going to find out if we in Western Canada suffered from this exclusively. I accordingly visited a couple of grocery stores on Elgin street, and I found that you are suffering here from exactly the same conditions that we have to endure in Western Canada, because the manufacturers are not playing the game honestly with the consumers in Canada. A free trader might say that 'the manufacturers are taking advantage of their privileges under the high tariff. It is not necessary that they should be permitted to do this. It is quite evident that in the United States there were exactly the same kind of manufacturers as we have in Canada, and until quite recently those



American manufacturers were taking advantage of the consumers by selling them a much smaller quantity than the cans and packages were supposed to contain. As a consequence, the United States Government took vigorous steps which resulted in the enactment of the Pure Food and other laws compelling the manufacturers of that country to be honest. I am sorry to say that we in Canada have reached that point where, if we are to have honest trading, we shall have to compel our'manufacturers to do the right thing. I believe we have some honest manufacturers in Canada, but wn have some who are certainly not honest. In those grocery stores on Elgin street I bought two cans which I weighed. One of them weighed four pounds, one ounce, and the other one exactly four pounds. When I opened them up I found that the contents did not nearly come up to the top, and the net weight was short five * or; six ounces in each case, and wholesalers who deal in these things say that condition prevails throughout Western Canada. What is the result? Our Cana; dian manufacturers ought to waken up to the situation. The people of Western Canada are sensible people; they understand what they are doing; they are not a lot of ninnies-let the manufacturers make no mistake about that. They get two classes of goods, whatever article you may take, one of Canadian manufacture and the other of American manufacture. One is not under any law and is put up in any old way, being short five or six ounces, and the other, of American manufacture, the people know by experience will contain the quantity and the quality in accordance with the standard. What are they-going to do? Just what they have been doing for the last number of years.. They are going to buy the American goods, and the Canadian manufacturer will have to do without their market. That is largely why the Canadian manufacturers have not, in Western Canada, the market which they ought to have. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will this session press that Bill which he brought in a short time ago and which was rejected by the Senate, at the last session, because in that way we may compel those manufacturers to deal justly with the Canadian consumer. There is only one thing I should like the minister to do, and that is to give me the privilege of writing the penalty clause. If my request is acceded to, I can assure the House that those Canadian manufacturers will not the second time engage in such practices.

'Canadian manufacturers have not shown good business judgment in their dealings with the western market, because, if they had, the condition which undoubtedly does, prevail in the West would not exist. If a man goes to Regina which, I believe, is the largest distributing centre of agricultural implements in the world-if not the largest it is very nearly the largest-he will find a most peculiar condition. He will find that, from now on for the rest of the season, warehouses will start filling up with machinery of all kinds which will overflow into the yards and will eventually cover acres upon acres of ground outside. Trainload after trainload of agricultural machinery is brought in, binders, tractors and everything else, and if you inspect them, you will find that they are almost all of American manufacture. I am fully convinced that Canadian machinery is equally as good as American and that being the case, how is it that American goods command the market as they undoubtedly do to-day, and why is it that Canadian manufacturers are not succeeding in the West? Canadian manufacturers should look into their methods, because American manufacturers have them beaten. Canadian manufacturers have undoubtedly indulged in very small and petty practices. If you go into a store and receive courteous treatment, you want to go back; but if you find that indefinable something or other that is repulsive, you do not return. Canadian manufacturers have not dealt generously and in a businesslike way with the people of Western Canada, and that is causing our people to deal with American manufacturers. It is just as well to recognize the truth. The facts are plain to anybody who goes to the West and sees the conditions or who studies the returns. I do not want to see that state of things continue, and I say to the Canadian manufacturers :	You must do more than fire a
whole lot of sarcastic references at long range at the western farmer.
That market must be regained, and sarcastic references to the people of Western Canada will not help to regain it. There must be no further indulgence in sarcasm of any sort and you must get down to a proper business basis, adequately paying your employees in Western Canada to look after your business instead of half paying them as is now the case. Dealers in agricultural implements in Canada working for Canadian firms are getting just above one-half of what is being paid by American business firms to dealers out there. I will give an illustration or two in regard to the methods that are being pursued. Not long

ago my wife gave me a list of goods she wanted ordered. I went into a store and asked for a certain article. The clerk informed me that it was not in stock, and when I reminded him that it used to be kept he admitted that it was but said they had a substitute that was just as good. It was American made, and I naturally wanted to know why the other, which was Canadian, was not sold. He said: "They advertised that all over the town the other day at ten cents and the price is fifteen cents." I asked him, then, if he would not sell more of that article at ten cents. He said, "Yes, but we get six cents profit on this article whereas on the other we get only one cent." Now, that was a strange situation, but it is the fact. American manufacturers largely have the western market to-day because they are giving to the Western Canadian dealers a much larger percentage of commission for handling their goods than the Canadians give, with the result that the dealers press American goods wherever they can. I shall now mention a case that is not by any means recent, in order to show that this condition has existed for quite a long while. When I landed in Regina thirty years ago from the city of Guelph, which was my ow*n home town, I wanted to buy a sewing machine. I picked out a "Raymond" which happened to be manufactured in my own city, and of which fact I ivas naturally proud. The dealer told me that they had a "Raymond" at $35, but he showed me another machine which he declared to he much better and the price of which was $65. One was American and- the other Canadian. He talked me into buying the $65 American machine, and about two months afterwards, on our meeting on the street, he inquired as to how the machine had worked. I said it was all right, but that my wife was emphatic in the opinion that it was no better than the other machine. He said: It may not be better to you, but it is worth $30 more to me. [DOT]I asked him what he meant, and he replied that there was just that much more profit to him in urging the sale of the American machine. Could you expect anything else than that he would endeavour to the best of his ability to sell that machine? These are the business methods that obtain all over Western Canada. Canadians are being done out of their own market by reason of the fact that the manufacturers of Eastern Canada have not studied conditions and have made no serious attempt to retain that trade. I make 2214
that statement without any hesitation because there is no question about the truth of it.
Before the hon. member leaves that point will he tell us what commission Americans pay and what commission Canadian manufacturers pay their agents?
It depends on the goods. Does the hon. gentlemen mean agricultural implements?
Yes. The hon. member says the Americans pay a much higher commission to their agents than do the Canadians.

I shall come to that in a few moments and answer the hon. member absolutely. I have a letter from a manufacturer's agent in Nebraska who says that implement dealers in the United States are paid 20 per cent by American implement firms.
'Mr. W. H. WHITE: And what about Canadian dealers?

I shall answer that presently. There are a few matters to which I wish to refer and before I am through I shall answer the hon. member's question. I have here the result of an inquiry conducted by the Retail Merchants' Association of Western Canada, a body that is not at all prejudiced. I take it that the association is anxious to get down to a solid business basis, and I shall read a part of the findings of the investigation. Now, this seems to me to prove that the people of Western Canada have a real grievance. We do not want to be ugly, but we find that we are suffering and our suffering is reacting on Canadian business to its injury. We want to have this condition of things remedied as speedily as possible, because, as we are all Canadians, it is desirable that we should arrive at some understanding satisfactory to both the manufacturers and the dealers, and we see no reason why this should not be done.
We do not want to coerce these manufacturers at all, but I want to know why this extraordinary increase has taken place east of the Great Lakes, while there has been -a reduction in working expenses and cost west of the Great Lakes. I am mighty glad that the Finance Minister has decided to give us that inquiry. I would urge that he make that inquiry as quickly as he possibly can.
I have far exceeded my time, but I am going to deal with just one other subject altogether different from this. There is a great deal of discontent in Western Canada with the conditions at present prevailing. I do not wonder at it. I am going to tell you
