At six
o'clock I was pointing out that, having regard to the conditions which have prevailed during a number of years, certain large concerns and avenues of trade in this country should -be brought under the control of the Government. I was saying that this should be done because the Government is supposed to have only one object and one purpose in view, the general advantage and the general benefit otf the * people; and if such control as I have suggested was exercised over such things as transportation, grain elevators, and cold storage plants, the Government would be able to prevent profiteering and undue exactions from the people. Had the Government kept under their hand the cold storage plants particularly, profiteering in foodstuffs would not have taken place to the extent that it did and would not have got beyond the control of the Gvernment,
I was pointing out also that several warnings had been given to the Government in this regard, but that the Government had declined to take any action of material advantage to the people. The conditions to which I have referred still prevail; very high prices are charged for the necessities of life. It is to -be hoped that even at this late day the Government will take action by carrying out the recommendations o-f the report, which we hope will be received in a -few days, from the commission presided over by Judge Mathers. Although we have no knowledge of what that report, will be, we have been observing the nature of the evidence that has been presented to the commission, and if the report is based upon the evidence as we see it, it should recommend that some steps be taken by the -Government in the general interests of the country and with a view to relieving the burdens of the poor people who find it extremely difficult at

this time to provide the necessary sustenance for their families.
The watchword of the Minister of Finance is, "produce and -save." That advice is, o-f course, very proper for all times. It is a tenet of religion that everything should be done decently and in order, and that nothing should be wasted. In the days of the miracle of the loaves and fishes, the Master him-self instructed the people to pick up the cru-mbs that were left over and to see that nothing -was lost; so that in asking us to produce and to save, the Minister of Finance is following a very excellent precedent. But it is a rather sad fact that the Government themselves are not setting a very good example in the way of saving and husbanding the moneys of the people.
At this stage I should remind the Government of something that appears very much to the outsider as a leakage in connection with the Department of the Overseas Military Forces. It was reported in the newspapers, and asserted in this House, that in one branch of that department an investigation had revealed a shortage of $10,000,000. That is a large amount of money, and if the loss really took place, if there was a defalcation, or whatever it might be called, to that extent in connection with the management of that department, a full explanation should be given. A question with regard to the matter was submitted to the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mew-burn) some time during this session, and his answer was, as I recollect it, that the matter did. not come under his department, but that when the Minister of Overseas Military Forces (Sir Edward Kemp) returned to Canada he would make a statement and these matters would be explained. The Minister of the Overseas Military Forces returned and made a very full statement indeed covering the activities of his department. We listened with interest to see whether he was going to explain this reported leakage or loss of $10,000,000, but he sat down without saying anything at all about it. The member for Maisonneuve, (Mr. Lemieux) who had previously made reference to the matter, asked the Minister of the Overseas Military Forces if he had any explanation to make regarding this Jenkins' report, as it was called, but I do not think that the minister gave any information on the subject; my recollection is that he said nothing about it. Questions were asked about it in the House, and a return to an Order of the House was brought down the other day which was supposed to

be an answer to the inquiries which have been made. I have read that return, Sir, and I find nothing in it which is an explanation about the Jenkins' report or which gives any information concerning this $10,000,000 which is said to have been lost. I submit that when $100 is supposed'to be lost, the fullest explanation should be given to the people; much more should the fullest possible explanation be given when such a large sum as $10,000,000 is supposed to have been lost in connection with one branch of the public service. This is only one thing that happened to come to the surface. We heard about it: we read about it and we tried to get information that would be satisfactory to the people, but so far we have obtained none. I bring the matter again to the notice of the Government. I do not say whether or not the report is true; all I say is that it appeared in the newspapers and that questions were put concerning it to the minister, who made no explanation. The return which was brought down and which was supposed to explain the whole matter away does not at all explain it, and things stand as they were. 1 suggest that the Government, which, through the Minister of Finance, gives us the very sage, the very wise and proper advice, "produce and save," take a little more care in the saving end of it so far as the money of the people is concerned.
As to production in this country, the Government, of course, is not called upon to produce, it is the business of the people in the various callings and walks of life to produce. Whatever profession or calling a man chooses in life he owes a duty to that profession or to that calling. If a man is a doctor, he ought to make the most of his profession; he ought to be an ornament to it -and the same is true of all the professions. If a man chooses to be a farmer, it is his duty to devote all his talent and ability to the high and honourable calling which he has chosen and to be successful in it if he can. It is the duty of the Government to encourage the different walks and callings of life, the different professions and industries, the different sources of production, whatever they may be, and, as far as it is possible to do so, to put means within the reach of the people so that the proper kind of men and women will have equal opportunities in a free country like ours. That is the doctrine which I would preach to the Government when they ask us to produce and to save.
It is just as important to cultivate the fisheries of the country as it is to cultivate the farms.
We have on the Atlantic and the Pacific immense fishery resources, and it is within the power of the Government to do a great deal for the development of our fisheries. We speak often and properly of building railways through the wheat fields in the West, and it is right and fitting that the wheat fields and granaries of the West should be traversed and touched by our railway lines and every other suitable means of transportation. But it is equally fitting that the fishery grounds and the fishing villages, towns and centres of this Dominion should also be put in touch with lines of railway. In parts of British Cblum-bit, which have no railway facilities, we have magnificent fisheries, and it is highly desirable that they should have railways for the proper development of that industry. In my province of Nova Scotia, and in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, we have magnificent fishing centres, but they are far away from railway lines, and it is impossible to carry on the industry with the advantage to the country that would be possible if better means of land transportation were available. There is no good reason why that magnificent fish food which we have in abundance in Nova Scotia should not be placed on the table of the man in Toronto, or Quebec, or Montreal, or any other great city, in the same shape as it leaves the water, if suitable facilities by way of cold storage and refrigerator cars were provided. Those are encouragements which the Government can give, and by giving them for the benefit of the fisheries and other industries, the Government will be doing something that will encourage our workers, whether fishermen, fanners or lumbermen to put energy into the businesses in which they are engaged. Those are the things which the Government should bear in mind when they are giving us advice in Canada to "produce and to save." There was never a time in the history of this great country of ours when it was so necessary and desirable as it is now to produce and to save.
There is another thing that must be done if we are to have the best results from the citizenship of this country. A man must be a free citizen in this country; he must be taught to love his country. He must be given to understand that he is in a country of equal opportunities of equal advantages, and that once he places his feet upon the soil of Canada and behaves himself as he ought to, observing our laws, he is entitled



to the heritage which has been handed down to us by generations of development and to the fullest of civilization in this country. That is another of the great facts which ought to be brought home to the minds and hearts of the people who are to develop this country and to produce ana to save, if this country is to be what it should be. I have in mind people in this country who are British subjects and who are not getting the benefits which are supposed to flow from that great legacy. We have on our Statute Book a law, namely, chapter 77 of the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1906, section 24 of which says:
An alien to whom a certificate of naturalization is granted shall, within Canada, be entitled to all political and, other rights, powers and privileges, and be subject to all obligations, to which a natural-born British subject is entitled or subject within Canada, with this qualification, that he shall not, when within the limits of the foreign state of which he was a subject previously to his obtaining his certificate of naturalization, be deemed to be a British subject, unless he has ceased to be a subject of that state in pursuance of the laws thereof, or in pursuance of a treaty or convention to that effect.
That is the promise of this Parliament, put in the shape of a solemn statute, passed by the House of Commons and the Senate, assented to by the Crown and spread broadcast throughout the world, inviting immigrants to come to this country. They came to this country; they qualified for the taking of the oath which they must take before they are naturalized, and when they are naturalized, they come within the purview of this law. I am sorry to say that, notwithstanding that law which is on our statute-book to-day, and has been on our statute-book for many years past, we have refused the right of citizenship to hundreds of thousands of people within this country within the last three or four years. I hope the Government will realize that the time has come when that blot caused by what is familiarly known as the War-time Elections Act, by which thousands of people who had this promise in their hand and who had earned this right were deprived of that privilege, should no longer remain upon the escutcheon of the Canadian people or the Canadian Government, and that we should once more go back to the time when we regarded ourselves as bound by our laws and recognized that our promises were absolutely and finally binding upon us, that the promise of a minister should not be doubted, much less the promise of the country and that no statute should be disregarded by any Government or individual. There is nothing that I stand by more

firmly than constitutional government, and I assure the Prime Minister and the Government that if there is anything necessary from this side of the House to assist them in maintaining law and order and constitutional usages in this country, they shall find .the most devoted and loyal support from hon-. gentlemen on this side. But lei me remind hon. gentlemen that when we have instances of this kind, when we have governments and officials of governments shying round statutes and doing things which should not be done, they must not be surprised if, in particular, strangers coming into this country should rather hesitate and not have the same regard for our laws, institutions and conduct generally in matters of government that they would otherwise have. If we are going to assimilate the hundreds of thousands of people who are coming into 'Canada; if we are going to make them proper Canadians it is absolutely essential that we should show them an example. They should see in us a peace-loving, God-fearing, law-abiding, honest people, and should understand that the people who come into this country are expected to measure up to our standards. But if they find after they come here that notwithstanding this heritage of ours we do not live up to the high ideals that it sets before us, then we must not he surprised if these people are not the excellent citizens that we should expect them to be.
I desire to say a word or two in regard to the present labour difficulties in this country. I do not purpose to go extensively into that question just now, for I believe that it is possibly not the best time to discuss it. One may say something that may be misunderstood, hut I would say to the Government, for all that, that I rather think that its attitude and that of the ministers who went to the great centre of labour at Winnipeg to deal with the difficulties there was rather of an unkind and unsympathetic nature, and that, in my judgment at all events, they have not exercised the very scrupulous care and excellent judgment necessary in dealing with such a question as confronted them there. I fear, whether reasonably or not, that the labour people or those who are in trouble out there, regard the ministers as being entirely on one side of the question and out of sympathy with those out on strike. I suppose it is impossible for the Government to bring about very satisfactory results if those on one side of the dispute have reached the conclusion that the Government are unfriendly to ithem and are not disposed to give them a fair

show. We were dealing with this question of labour a few days ago. I said then, and I say now, as a friend of labour and as a man who has been brought up among labourers and who in this House represents a very large body of labouring men, that I was, and am still, anxious that some easy, proper and lasting way should be found by which troubles of this kind in this country should be dealt with in a satisfactory constitutional way, in order that they may be prevented as far as possible. I submit, Sir, that it is impossible (to obtain efficiency in dealing with labour problems or in adjusting labour difficulties by means of temporary boards. You have a board to-day to deal with a case, say, in the city of Quebec. You have three of the very best men you can get and perhaps they will settle the question. Probably they may never have sat on a board before, and may not sit on such a board again for twenty years, if ever. They are absolutely new men, untrained, and in all probability know nothing about the business in hand. Every time you form a board you have raw-recruits who are unacquainted with the conditions that have to be considered, who are absolutely untrained, and may be somewhat indifferent about their responsibilities -regarding their work as a small job and not attaching to it the importance which it deserves. They feel that once they have disposed of the question before them there is an end of their labours. What sort of administration of justice would we have in this country if the Supreme Court of Canada, for example, were constituted of three or four men whom you might pick up on the street to sit for a few days and try cases and who, when that was over, would never meet again? Apply the same rule to the different courts. (Suppose you had untrained men without an adequate knowledge of the law, and not properly equipped, to deal with the cases that might come before them from time to time, and what would be the state of the administration of our law? That, however, is not the case. On our benches in the different provinces, and in the Supreme Court of Canada, there are trained jurists who have given their lives to the study of law and evidence and are well versed in the proper application of the rules of evidence. As a result we have careful trials and, as a rule, proper and equitable decisions. Now, Sir, my view is that if it is necessary in dealing with problems in every day life that we should have trained men who understand the business of law and who have made its study their life 222i
work, it is equally proper and necessary, when we come to deal with the great questions involved in the relation that exists between millions of men engaged in labour and hundreds of thousands of capitalists, that we should have some method by which men adequately qualified for the work should be able to deal with all matters that come before them, in the difficulties that arise from time to time in a systematic way that would be satisfactory to all concerned.
I made this statement the other day in this House, and some newspapers and individuals jumped to the conclusion that I was unfriendly to labour and wanted to constitute	a	court	that would
force men to accept its findings. I was accused of being altogether one-sided. I am nothing of the kind and to-night, after due consideration of what I said before, I say that not many years will pass by before hon. gentlemen sitting in this House and public men in the country will have reached the conclusion that it was surprising that we did not long ago take some proper step along this line. I submit to you, Sir, as I submitted the other night, that possibly it would not be a good thing to make a court of this kind compulsory at the outset. But if such a court were constituted and for some years at least it were left to the option of interested parties to go to it or not as they chose, I am sure that those who resorted to it would find it so satisfactory and so far superior to strikes as a means of settling labour questions that it would not be far in the future when everybody would take his difficulties to it.. In Nova Scotia there is a body known as the Utilities Board, and perhaps there is such a board in every other province. When difficulties arise in Nova Scotia they are taken to this board. Any difficulty between the consumers of electric light, for instance, and the company is not permitted to be settled by a strike. The aggrieved side express their difficulties in writing and the document is handed in to the chairman or the secretary of the Utilities Board. A copy of the petition is served to the other side, and within ten or twenty days they send their answer. If they cannot agree a day is fixed for hearing the case, and the whole matter is thrashed out, and an order is made by the board binding on all parties concerned. If a similar system-I do not say the same system -were adopted in connection with strikes, I am sure the result would be satisfactory.
I am in favour of unions and I think that all labour in the country should be well

united under proper leadership. But, while I favour labour unions and their proper administration, I must say that I have no use whatever for the agitator or the fire-eater who makes a business of stirring up strife and trouble. However, when all labour is properly organized I can see no difficulty in the way of any body of united labour putting their complaints in writing and filing them with a proper tribunal which could submit them to the employer and obtain his answer. If the answer were deemed unsatisfactory the tribunal could appoint a time for both parties to appear and discuss the matter in dispute with a view to settlement. I think that is what is coming in the future. We may not see it to-day or to-morrow, but the day will *come "when disputes in this country, whether of labour or otherwise, will not be left to the haphazard arbitration of strikes. I am sure that no men desire to go on strike if they can get their difficulties satisfactorily settled otherwise, and as it is to-day we are not offering to the people -anything that will settle their difficulties. Let this Government take the view I present and adopt such a court as I have suggested. They could leave lit, for some .years at all events, to the judgment of the people whether they would have their difficulties solved by the tribunal, but 'the court would be there to settle disputes that might be taken to it.
This, Sir, is the view which I submitted before and which I present now. I do not want to introduce any personal matter but I wish to bring to the notice of the right lion, the Prime Minister that, since I made that statement before, one of the commissioners on Judge Mathers' commission busied himself as a street corner politician in the city of Sydney trying to arouse feeling against me because I made the statement in this House a few days ago. If this is the class of men that they send around the country to promote peace, order and good government, they are making a mistake. It does not concern me very much, but I am sure that that is neither the wish nor the will of the Government and that they would not desire any person who goes around the country, paid by the Government and supposed to be acting for the people, to convert himself into a political machine and try to stir up trouble against me or any member of this House in any section of the country.
I do not know why there should be any misunderstanding, or any lack of confi-klence, between, any body of people in this

country and the Government of the day. If there is such, the sooner the Government take steps to remove it, and give everybody, whether employer or employed, to understand that it is the function of governments in this country to deal fairly and squarely with all interests whether of the capitalist or of the man whose only capital is his brain and the strength of his arm, the better it will be.
Along the lines of assisting labour and helping production in this country, I would remind the Government, once more that the coal industry in Nova Scotia depends largely upon shipping. On account of the war, the shipping oil which we depend was shut off. We do not complain of that; nor do we complain of anything else necessary to advance the interests of the country in the war. But the war was over on the 11th November, and three or four ships which were taken away from the Dominion Coal Company are not yet returned. It was thought by the owners of these ships, who are in the Old Country, that they were not obliged to return them because, as they alleged, the war cancelled their contract. The matter was tried out in the English courts and the judges held that the war did not cancel the contract and that the moment the war was over the ships were obliged to return to their old charters. But what has happened is that these shipowners, through some influence, and wishing to keep their ships in the service of the Government as long as possible, sent the ships off to Australia. From Australia they were sent to the Mediterranean, and kept a-way from their proper contracts possibly until now. I do not know whether this Government could have intervened to compel-possibly not compel, but advise-the Home Government to send these ships back to their proper charters. What happened was that we in Nova Scotia lost the use of these ships, and as they were chartered before the war, the rates were reasonably low. If we had these ships it would enable us to place coal in Montreal and other places on the St. Lawrence at a reasonable price. As it is now, coal is selling high, and the people of Nova Scotia have not the facilities that these ships would afford them. The impression is that the Government have not done what they should and could have done in this matter. I am not saying whether or not that is true, but that is the impression, and possibly some day we shall find out what the full facts are. If it is true that the Government could have obtained these vessels for the company and sent them back for the

proper discharge of their contract under the charters, they should have done so. The reason why the owners of the ships continued them in the service of the Government was that they were getting very much larger freight rates and making a great deal more money out of their war-time charters than they would have made if they had carried out the old agreement with the coal company. However, the courts have decided that they were obliged to come back. It is a pity that they were allowed to remain away to the great detriment of the people in Nova Scotia who were depending upon them.
Much has been said about parties and party government in this House and elsewhere. I do not intend to close my remarks without making some observation along these lines. I do not mention party with the intention of casting the slightest possible reflection upon any person, whether he belongs to the Liberal party or the Conservative party. Parties are institutions in this country. We here have been governed for the last one hundred years, as they have for a longer period in the Old Country, along party lines and under the party system. Whatever development we have made in this country, whatever development they have made in England or the United States, or in any civilized country, has been made under party government. Therefore, party government, to my mind is an institution that should not hastily, or without due consideration, be set aside. Party lines and party government develop likes and dislikes; the likes are the things that we particularly prefer. Party creates traditions, love of men and love of country along lines which, in so far as I know, cannot otherwise be developed. It is not usually easy for one to cut himself away from the ties of party and party government. Particularly is that the case where we find properly conducted party government. I am sure, Sir, that the Conservatives of Canada-the old-line and the new-line Conservatives-would be sorry indeed to be deprived of the lustre, honour and glory that they have derived, or which they take to themselves, by being connected with a party with which are associated such names as those of the Right Hon. 'Sir John Macdonald, the Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper, and the Right Hon. Sir John Thompson. My hon. friends opposite, 1 am sure, will be. pleased to remember that . they were friends, supporters and partisans of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden), who leads the House to-day. On
this side of the House, I know we shall always be proud of such names as George Brown, Sir Oliver Mowat, Alexander Mackenzie, and, last, but not least, the great . and distinguished gentleman who led us until yesterday-I might say-the Right -Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. These are names and traditions which are worthy of being perpetuated. Whatever may have happened during the war-I am not saying a word about that just now-I think that the growth and development of this country should be along party lines.
J am not, of course, saying anything new when I say that. It. has been already stated in this House in a very eloquent and interesting speech by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) has also made a similar statement,
I say now, as I have said 'before, though not with the idea of making the slightest reflection against any hon. gentleman whether he sits on this side or on the opposite side of the House, that following along party lines offers the best system of government that has yet been discovered in this country. People who think they are very smart in uttering clever things may talk about severing that, this and the other thing from politics. It is impossible in Canada to sever things from polities-that is, politics in the proper sense. There is a sense in which politics are spoken of sneeringly, and in connection with the lowest things that can happen in this country, but it is for men such as the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government to lift polities, government, and political parties above such sneers, and to place them on the high plane on which they ought to be. Men would respect him and: others if they would take that high stand and continue it. '
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal further, and shortly, with the attitude of the Liberal, party as far as regards trade and the trade questions of this country. That is nothing new, it is well known, but in view of something that I mentioned this afternoon and some use that was made of my own. name throughout the country, some reference to it on my part becomes necessary. If I. were merely a private member, I would not for a moment bother about noticing it at aUf. but occupying the position that I now do there is perhaps exaggerated attention paid' to anything I say. Whatever may happen to me personally, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that while I occupy this position I am particularly anxious that no word, or act of

mine should in the slightest way whatever reflect on the party to which I belong, or interfere in the slightest way with the confidence with which that party is regarded by the people of the Dominion. For that reason, Sir, I wish to make perfectly clear my own attitude with regard to the trade issue. But I might first revert for a moment to the question of production to which I made reference a few minutes ago. Production is not a local question. The production of flour, or the production of wheat, although it takes place on a great scale in the West is not a western question. It is one in which everybody in Canada is concerned because wheat and flour constitute the food of the people, and when the food of the people is the matter a't issue that of course is a national question. When we are asked to do anything that will help the farmer in the West, if the giving to him of free implements is going to help him, that is not for himself alone, it is for the industry in which he is concerned, it is in the national interest, because it is hoped that greater production will follow, and that the results will find their way through the channels of industry to the consumer. Therefore, when we are called upon to help the farmers in the West in getting implements for them to plant their grain and harvest it, when we are called upon to help the lumberman in his production of lumber, or to help the miner and the fisherman in their respective callings so that they may produce more, we are not doing that exclusively in their interest-we are doing it for them of course, but in the greater cause of the general interest of the country. That, Sir, is the position we take on this side of the House, and always take when we announce ourselves in favour of making conditions easy either for the people in the West or for producers all over the country. The taunt always thrown across the floor of the House is that we on this side have not lived up to the position which we took in 1893 when the great Liberal convention was held in this city-that .Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his followers did not adhere to the promise that they gave at that time. The assertion has been made thousands of times all over the country that Sir Wilfrid Laurier on that occasion said we were going to have free trade as it was in England. Sir Wilfrid Laurier never said anything of the kind. I will quote his actual remarks at Ottawa in 1893 when the resolution referring to that matter was before the convention :
[Hr. McKenzie.]
I say the policy should he the policy of free trade such as they have in England.
I am sorry to say that the circumstances of the country cannot admit at present of that policy in its entirety, but I speak to you from this day forward that it should be the goal to which we aspire. I propose to you from this day forward, although we cannot adopt the policy itself, to adopt the principle which regulates it . That is to say, that though it should be your misfortune for many years to come to have to raise the revenue by customs duties, those duties should be levied only so far as is necessary to carry on the business of the government. Nothing is more difficult,-that is one of the evils of protection-than to wipe away protection because under it interests have been established which every man who has at heart the interest of all classes must take into consideration. It is always easy to increase the *tariff because by doing so you increase the private fortunes of certain individuals, but whenever you decrease the tariff it has always to be done with careful consideration, and I am sure that when the Liberals are in power they will not be indifferent to this primary consideration.
That, Sir, is all that the late Eight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, and that was the principle enunciated by him at that time and which he always followed. It will therefore appear to you, Sir, how unfair it was and how unfair it is to-day, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier should be charged with saying we were going to have free trade as it was in England, and that he never carried out his promise. I submit, Sir, that what I have given is the text and the guide of the Liberal party to-day, following along the lines as laid down by the great chieftain at that time. Although he is gone, his memory and his principles and what he has done for this country, will not easily depart from the recollections of those who had the great honour of being close to him during- his lifetime, and particularly during his public career.
I have said here before, and I repeat it, that speaking for myself I have always supported the resolutions that were passed, or proposed, in this House, looking to the forwarding of this principle as laid down by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. On the 28th of January, 1914, the then member for Humboldt, Mr. Neely, moved this resolution:
That the House regrets that, in the gracious Speech with which Your Royal Highness has met Parliament, the said Speech gives no indication of any intention on the part of your Advisers to take any steps to secure free access to the markets of the United States for the wheat and wheat products of Canada by removing the duty on wheat and wheat products coming into Canada from the United States.
That resolution was put to a vote in this House and myself and others- on this side voted for it. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House voted against it.

On the 23rd of April, 1914, the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved this resolution :
That this House is of the opinion that in view of the prevailing economic conditions of the country it is1 advisable to place wheat, *wheat products', and agricultural implements on the free list; and that without doing injustice to any class, steps should toe taken to alleviate the high cost of living toy considerate removal of taxation.
On that occasion every Liberal in the House voted for the resolution, and our Conservative friends to a man voted against it.
On the 16th of March, 1916, the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved this resolution :
That this House is ready to provide for the exigencies of the present situation, and to vote all necessary ways and means to that end, but it regrets Chat in the measure under consideration duties are imposed which may toe oppressive on the people, whilst yielding little or no revenue; and that the said measure is particularly objectionable in the fact that instead of favouring, it is placing extra barriers against Great Britain's trade with Canada, at a moment when the Mother Country is under a war strain unparalleled in history.
That resolution was voted for by every Liberal member, and voted against by hon. gentlemen supporting the Government and by the Government themselves.
On the 23rd of February, 1916, the then member for Assiniboia, now Hon. Senator Turriff, moved this resolution:	*
That in, the opinion of this House, in order to secure the farmers and people of Canada the advantages of the American market for wheat products and potatoes, steps should toe taken at once to put these articles on the free list in the Canadian tariff.
For that resolution hon. gentlemen on this side of the House voted, and hon. gentlemen supporting the Government and the Government themselves voted against it.
On the 23rd of May, 1917, the then member for Edmonton, Hon. Frank Oliver, moved this resolution:
That in the opinion of this' House it would be in the public interest if the Customs Tariff Act were so amended as to provide;
1. That wheat, wheat flour and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list;
2- That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour, and sawmill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oil, cement and fertilizers, be added to the free list;
3.	That staple goods and food (products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and food therefor be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty;
4.	That substantial reductions be made in the general tariff on all articles imported into Canada, excepting luxuries;
5.	That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
For that resolution all the Liberal members voted, and hon. gentlemen supporting, the Government and the Government themselves voted against it.
On the 25th of March, 1919, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) moved a resolution. I do not know if 9 p.m. there is any objection to my reading it. It is not*from Hansard, it is a copy I possess. If there is no particular objection I would like to put it on Hansard. That resolution reads as follows:
Whereas in order to meet the great expenditure necessitated by our national obligation it is imperative that the labour and capital of this country should be directed to the obtaining of the greatest economic return, and that the energies of our people should be freed in order that the most be made of our natural resources and the strength and intelligence of our people be utilized to the fullest extent; and
Whereas it is advisable in the public interest that taxation should be borne by those most capable of sustaining the burden, and that the proceeds of taxation should reach the national exchequer, and should not be diverted into the hands of the privileged classes of the community ; and
Whereas the reciprocal trade agreement negotiated with the Government of the United States in January, 1'9H1, has been accepted by that Government, and legislation providing for its coming into force upon its acceptance by the Canadian Government has been passed by the said Government of the United States; and
Whereas the said agreement, providing as it does for the free interchange of the products of the farm, the sea, the mine and the forest, and for the freer exchange of many articles of prime necessity and universal use, offers to the producers and consumers of this country an opportunity which wisdom and patriotism demand should be availed of:
Therefore be it resolved that it is the opinion of this House :-
(a)	That the increases of duties of 7J per cent and 5 per cent enacted by the statute 5 George V. Chap. 3 should be repealed;
(b)	That the offer of reciprocity contained in the reciprocal trade agreement now upon the statute books of the United States of America should be immediately accepted in its entirety, and that legislation for that purpose should be introduced forthwith ;
(c)	That without derogation from the provisions of paragraph (b) hereof, all staple food and food products not now free (with the exception of luxuries), and domestic animals and foods therefor should be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty ;
(d)	That without derogation from the provisions of paragraph Ob) hereof, all farm and garden implements, machinery and tools, including farm tractors; all mining, flour and sawmill machinery and repair parts therefor, as well as the raw material entering into the same; lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils,

cement and fertilizers be added to the free lists-it being understood that the tariff benefit proposed to be conferred upon raw material entering into the manufacturing of the articles above set forth may be granted by way of rebate or drawback; it always being provided that in the event of any difference o.f duty existing under the provisions of different parts of this resolution, the lower duty or freedom from duty prevail;
(e)	That having regard always to the requirements of the public revenue and the necessity of affording reasonable opportunities for adjustment to those affected by the proposed changes, substantial reduction should toe made in the tariff with tho object of reducing the burden upon th<f consumer in respect of the prime necessities of life, and with the object of delivering the consumer from the bondage now imposed upon him by the exactions of monopolies, trusts, and combines.
That resolution was supported by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and voted against solidly by hon. gentlemen opposite, supporters of the Union Government.	_
There has been a great deal of talk that we on this side of the House moved that resolution because we were after the Unionists from the West, that we wanted to get them into trouble by forcing them to vote against that resolution. Nothing was further from the mind of any member of the Opposition. During the first session there was plenty o.f opportunity for us to move resolutions if we wanted to get our friends on the other side into difficulty, hut we simply left them alone. This year our friends everywhere were taunting us that we had not the courage to bring down any resolution at all.
Our only alternative, therefore, was to maintain our stand, to bring down that resolution and to ask hon. gentlemen to vote for or against it as they thought proper. But I protest against the suggestion that we supported this resolution because we wanted to get our western friends on the other side into trouble; because we wanted to get them " in wrong," so to speak, with their friends in the West. Nothing was further from our minds. It is being suggested now that we should have introduced a resolution similar to the first resolution introduced by the member for Brome, word for word. The rules of the House would not permit us to do that; we had to keep as far away from the first resolution as we could. If we did not propose the McMaster resolution word for word, it was simply because the rules of the House would not permit our doing so. Taking the responsibility of the position which I occupy for the moment, I say that the principles enunciated in the resolution submitted by the member for IBrome on 'March 25, are bind-
[ Mr. McKenzie. ]
ing upon us, and that we stand by every line, every word, every syllable and every thought in that resolution. It is the resolution which we would have submitted, if we could have done so, as an amendment to the motion made by the Minister of Finance. But let no one say that we are taking shelter under any subterfuge or trying to. get away from the iMcMaster resolution- nothing of the kind. Accordingly, I put myself on record as supporting the McMaster resolution of to-day and as coupling with it, as far as I can, the resolution which he moved and which we on this side voted for on March 25 last-a resolution which contains the views on trade and tariff questions which were entertained by the great chief himself, Sir Wilfrid OLaurier. Let me read the amendment now before the House, as moved by the member for Brome:
That all the words after the word "that" be left out, and the following inserted instead thereof:-
The proposals of the Finance Minister are unsatisfactory. They offer no curto against extravagance. They utterly fail to take any adequate steps to relieve the present high cost of living. They give no definite promise of tariff revision downwards.
That to relieve the present situation, the tariff should toe so framed as to free the food of the people and the machinery used1 in the development of the natural resources of Canada, together with the raw material entering into the manufacture thereof;
To take off or substantially reduce, as speedily as may be expedient and just to all interested, the duties upon all other necessaries of life;
Also, the reciprocal offer of trade with the United States should be accepted, and a general downward revision of the tariff undertaken forthwith in conformity with the principle herein enunciated.
That resolution, Sir, contains in concrete form the principles which we hold respecting matters of trade and tariff reform in this country. Nothing is further from the minds of the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House than to do what is vulgarly called "play the hull in the china shop" in regard to any of the industries of this country. We realize that we have to deal with principles, with institutions, with vested rights, and we assure the country at large that as the Liberal party has been capable in the past of dealing with questions of trade and of tariff and with matters affecting the general interests of the country, it is not now without the talent, the ability and the energy to do the same thing whenever the people of the country call upon it.
Now that the war is over, I hope that we, in common with other countries, shall profit by the lessons o'f the war. Let us hope that the great sacrifices offered on

the plains of France and Flanders shall not have been in vain; that the graves and crosses which mark these sad and sorrowful fields shall cause us to realize that as we have fought in other lands for freedom of thought, freedom of action, brotherly love, and brotherly conduct, so should we in our own country, carry out these principles and ideals. Let us hope that the possession of the name "Canadian," and of the qualities and attributes of a true Canadian, may entitle one to anything that is in the gift of the country. It would be a sad commentary upon the civilization of this country if a man who possessed the necessary qualifications for any high and important office should be debarred from obtaining it because of the church to which he belongs, because of the altar or shrine at which he worships his God. Let it not be said that any man is shut out or cut off from any high position for which God and nature intended him, simply because, forsooth, he happens to belong to this or that church. If the war shall have been instrumental in causing us to have that high spirit; if it causes us to uphold the principle that a man should stand upon his merits, that people should be judged by their worth, by what they are capable of doing for their home and their country, then all our sacrifices of blood and treasure shall not have been in vain.
Let me read to the House a very touching bit of composition that I saw in the Ottawa Journal of June 10:
Owen Wister, the American novelist a net author of that flaming- book "The Pentecost of Calamity," was in Westminster Abbey at the funeral service of Edith Cavel], and he sends to the Times these thoughts on that great ceremony :-
"In the hour of Edith Cavell's funeral service, as her body approached Westminster Abbey, but before it had quite reached the entrance, the waiting people thought it was come and rose in silent respect. During that silence, very faintly from above us as we stood, the clock struck noon.
"As I counted the strokes, these were my American thoughts :
"This woman, who died for her country, died for .more than that. The shots by which she fell killed what was left of the chance we should stay out of the fight. They tore away whatever was left of the veil that hid German savagery from our eyes.
"After that, it was merely a question of time when our bodies and our spirits should be equipped to join in defeating Germany.
"This Edith Cavell did; and now to-day, here conies her body, and we all, of many nations, but mostly of British race, rise to meet its approach.
"Presently the singing began, and my thoughts went on :-
"These words from the Bible that I am hearing, these prayers, this hymn, 'Abide with me,'
are the corner-stone of both my faith and my speech.
"This roof, where these words I have known by heart all my life are being uttered, is the shrine of my history. It belongs to me.
"It cannot he possible for any American, however untravelled hitherto, to enter here and linger awhile and learn what it holds, not to be stirred to his depths. The place speaks to him of himself, his meaning, his past, the great race to which he belongs.
"May the striking of that noon hour and the coming here of Edith Cavell's body mark the end of the era of misunderstanding and the beginning of the era of understanding between Great Britain and America."
That beautiful thought was put forward by that great writer, and I felt it would be well that I should bring it to the notice of this House and particularly to the notice of the Canadian people. If sacrifices like that of Edith Cavell struck this gentleman in such a way as to make him think it was a reason why all differences between Great Britain and the United States should forever disappear, should not the sacrifices of those united groups of English, Scotch, Irish and French, who, side by side on the fields of France and Flanders, having offered their hearts' blood for freedom, are united in death, and, we hope, united in heaven, be the cause of bringing about conditions of amity and understanding between those .different races and peoples in this country of ours? Let nobody he so small and narrow in thought and mind as in the future to look upon anybody, whether he be French, or Irish, or English, or Scotch, or whatever else he may be, as anything but a Canadian entitled to the mantle of love, charity and protection which we are prepared to throw over him if he is a worthy citizen under the Canadian flag.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address a few remarks to the House upon the Budget, I feel it is my first duty and privilege to extend congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) upon the able manner in which he has dealt with the fiscal questions that face us to-day. I realize thait every member of the House will not be in accord with those congratulations, but with the next remark I feel that a generous House will be in agreement, and that is to pay tribute to the Minister of Finance for the very able and untiring manner in which he has devoted his services to his country during the past few years that have been the most trying in our history. In dealing with the fiscal questions of ithe country he has, in my opinion, had his eye upon the main issues with which we are confronted.
