The argument is often put forward that many of our farmers have such a difficult time to get along that they are forced out of the farming occupation. It is true that a certain percentage do not make a success of farming, but I can present statistics to show that that condition does not pertain to farming alone. According to the returns made to Edward N. Hurley, ex-vice chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States, out of 250,000 trading and manufacturing concerns in the United States, over 100,000 earned no net returns whatever; in addition, 90,000 made less than $5,000 a year. However, when a business man fails, the fact is not brought to out attention as conspicuously as when a farmer abandons his farm. I would also like to point out that the furniture manufacturers of Ontario a few months ago issued a questionnaire and secured reports from fifty of the leading manufacturers in the province. These returns, which were correctly analyzed by a well known Toronto firm of chartered accountants, indicate that on an investment of nearly $12,0000,000 the return in 1917 was just over $300,000, or about two and-a-half per cent. The returns since 1917 have been somewhat better, but no one can rightly claim that the profits in this industry have been excessive, and the same can be said of many other groups of Canadian manufacturers.
Every real grievance should be removed from the farming or any other industry, and it is my desire to refute some of the extreme ideas that appear to prevail with regard to that one industry. The Minister of Finance has his sympathies in the right place; he has every desire, and rightly so, to see the agricultural industry put upon the soundest footing possible, because it is of prime importance to this country that it should be placed in that position.
May the attention of the hon. leader of the Opposition be called to an apparent error which he made when he referred to the resolution brought forward last March by the member for Brome? He stated that all the members on his side had voted for it. As a matter of fact two members spoke and voted against it, and some others refused to record their votes as they were not in harmony with it.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. leader of the Opposition with a great deal of interest and also with a great deal of sympathy, because I felt he was dealing with a very delicate question. Entire har-
[.Mr. Harold.]
mony upon this question does not dwell with our friends on your left, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) does not feel quite as free to deal with the facts and circumstances as he would if he were an independent member. When he referred to the ship which should be guided according to the various winds-which sounds logical enough-I could not help thinking that he had steered his own ship rather across the path of that of the hon. member for Brome, and had taken the wind out of his sails. But may this appeal be made to the hon. leader of the Opposition: That he recognize the facts and circumstances in connection with the implement industry and not register his vote in favour of the amendment? Because I believe that as good a case has been made out for this industry as1 he put forward for his coal and steel. He mentioned that no person could start up housekeeping without having the customary utensils, and those are necessities to the farmers and to the workingmen just as much as are farm implements; and as those utensils are granted a good measure of protection, it is incomprehensible to me how it can be reasoned that the same principle should not apply to other things. In fact, the attitude of some hon. members is influenced too much by the political propaganda carried on in the country.
There is another point to be mentioned- the " land taxation " scheme of the Council of Agriculture. Before the session closes may some one who can speak with authority explain just what is meant by that phrase. At a public meeting not long ago the Vicepresident of the United Farmers of Ontario put a different interpretation upon it than that of our friends from the West. They call for a direct tax on unimproved land, including all natural resources. If that means practically unoccupied land it will result in confiscation and very little revenue; but if it means the assessment of all land on an unimproved basis then we have something of an entirely different nature. Some figures have been given me dealing with the value of land in the various provinces, totalling $4,260,000,000. In some instances it has been impossible to separate the land from the buildings, and this figure is undoubtedly high. But if we were to take one-half of that as unimproved value it would be necessary to assess it at 6 per cent to get a revenue of $127,800,000. A farm valued at $8,000, and reduced to $4,000 on the basis of unimproved value, at 6 per. cent would return a tax of $240, or at 3 per cent $120. Every effort has been made to get

some definite statement with regard to this taxation, and in putting forth these figures I do so without being arbitrary, but simply to try and draw out some specific statement with regard to the question.
In arriving at that total valuation, did the hon. gentleman include all land, or only agricultural land?

These are assessed lands.
Mr. MAHARlG: That is, agricultural land?

All assessed land, city and agricultural-the total assessment. I do not wish to put myself on record as being opposed to a scheme of land taxation that will bring back to the state a proportion of unearned increment, but one will readily, see that with the different ideas prevailing in regard to this question it will not only take some time to arrive at a basis of taxation, but it will take a greater time to arrange a system of assessment and collection. Time is required, and as this Budget is only for one year, it does seem to me most reasonable to ask that that proposition be laid aside as impracticable until it is put forward in a more concrete form.
The general question of free trade and protection has. been debated for many hours. The debate has been a brilliant one and has not been a loss of time. The
10 p.m. general attitude towards it has been one looking to the national interest. We have different viewpoints, which is to be expected. I wish to place very briefly before the House my views on the general fiscal policy of the country. In the first place, we must recognize the principle that unity is absolutely necessary. In framing the next tariff stability should be one of the first things considered also. For many years to come the revenue will have to be derived in a very substantial way from 'the tariff. Another thing that should be considered is the desirability of developing the national wealth; and in that respect I am in full agreement with the leader of the Opposition, that there is not any heresy in our producing goods at home when we can do so on a basis that is fair and just to the different classes in .the community. Last, but not least, we have to consider the national spirit. Our provinces stretching from the Atlantic to tne Pacific are joined up by our great railways, and the national sentiment after the great war should be more in harmony with the ideals of this country than it could possibly have been before.
As our soldiers come home they leave the ranks of their various battalions, and some
go to the East and some to the West. It should be the desire of this country to adopt a policy that will unite these men and be fair and just to all.
A narrow or partisan feeling as against our great neighbour to the south is improper, but we must recognize the fact that she has made no departure from the fiscal policy which she has followed in the past, a policy which has been one of considering herself first. We must recognize that she is a great and powerful country, and that at the present time we are heavily indebted to her. We should try to put ourselves in such a position that we shall be able to ease up that burden. The right way to do that is to make ourselves self-contained, so far as that is possible. We should have a policy that will encourage home industry in all its various branches, and enable our own people to produce our own requirements, so far as we can do so equitably Under no circumstances would I subscribe myself as a high protectionist. I would not be any higher in that regard than our good friend the leader of the Opposition, although I would stand on his first position to-night rather than on the position which he took in the latter part of his speech.
With a view to bringing about unity, stability and good feeling, producing a revenue and upbuilding the country in a national way, the tariff should be so framed that we should have no extortion, no profiteering, no combinations. To arrive at that point, it is necessary that the tariff be not so high that the price prevailing outside this country for commodities would not regulate the prices for similar commodities in this country-this without departing from the principle that it is desirable to encourage the production of our home needs.
It was with regret that ll noticed that the member for Humboldt (Mr. Lang) in his most excellent address made the statement. that some of the people in the West were buying foreign goods in order that a revenue might thereby go direct to the Government, If hon. gentlemen would look at this question from a broader standpoint they would see that a very .large revenue does go to the Government in the amount represented by the duties which the makers pay, and that there is great benefit to this country in the freights to the West on our own Government railways and in the proportion of taxation whidh, in various forms, companies and their employees pay. They should also recognize the justice of

giving the home article the preference over the foreign article. Surely there is no heresy in that.
Our good friend the ex-iMinister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) cited the cream separator industry as an example of an industry flourishing in this country under free trade. I would like him to make an investigation of that' industry and of the patents and licenses which are controlled by it, which are a much greater source of protection than any tariff wall could be. We know some of these companies; their names are household words, and need not be mentioned. Some widely advertised cream separators are manufactured in this country by different concerns which are controlled by outside parent companies who will not allow their territory to be infringed upon. The illustration given by the Minister of Agriculture does not stand upon all fours with the general agricultural implement business.
The questions already dealt with are not all the.most important questions which confront the country at the present time. One of the most important issues that we have to face now is that of the maintenance of law in this country. It would be most regrettable if this House should show any uncertainty or any hesitation in maintaining our institutions or demonstrate any lack of faith in them at this time. Moreover, it is out of place that we should at this stage of the peace negotiations show any lack of confidence in those who represent us in these important negotiations. What would we think if Premier Clemenceau of France was turned out of power by the House of Deputies upon a tariff question at this time? It seems to me that if we should do anything of this kind we would cast a cloud upon all the war efforts and achievement of this country during the past five years.
In closing, this appeal is made to some of our friends who are thinking of leaving us at this time. May each of them place themselves in the position of sole judge of the Government and ask himself-indeed they cannot evade the question-whether he is willing at this time to take the responsibility of turning the Government out of power upon an issue of minor importance.
A short time ago the Prime Minister returned to this country from the scene of the peace negotiations and was welcomed by this House in a way which showed that he had the confidence of the House and especially of his followers. His burdens have been very great; he has fulfilled his responsibilities conscientiously and to the

very best of his ability. Does it seem right that at this stage the Cabinet should be appealed to, as they are leading our victorious army out of the fray, to capitulate, or its supporters in this House be asked to strike down their leaders?

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to analyze in detail the speech of the Hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White); that has been done by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in a manner which met with, the approval of members on this side of the House and, in my opinion, with the approval of the great majority of the people. In three or four matters mentioned by the minister, however, I was particularly interested, and to these I win refer.
The minister purposes increasing the income tax, and I believe this is a step in the right direction. Hon. members will recall that in the discussion that took place in this House last year on the Budget- the Minister of Finance was not here then -hon. members on this side urged that the income tax be increased to where it is being placed to-day. We are again urging that there be a further increase, and I am perfectly satisfied that if it be not brought down before this debate closes, the minister, in view of the financial condition of the country, will recognize, when he comes before the House with his Budget next year, the necessity for a further increase.
There is also a proposal to eliminate the double income tax. This is reciprocal legislation, perfectly fair and just, and it eliminates the possibility of residents in Canada having to pay two taxes. Many of our people living along the border had to bear this burden last year; this proposal will relieve them. The same may be said of the legislation enacted last year with reference to reciprocal tax exemption with the United States as regards smaller wage earners. This has worked out very satisfactorily, and the minister and his department did much with the United States Government at Washington to have them carry out as speedily and as promptly as they could what was intended to be done under the Act of 1918.
The minister in the course of his address dealing with the financial affairs of the country, stated that the national debt was approximately $2,000,000,000. He told us that of this sum $1,510,000,000 was held in the Dominion, and also that the last Victory Loan which was placed before the people last October amounted to approximately $700,000,000. As these bonds were issued free of income tax, it means

with that amount outstanding approximately $80,000,000 of income escapes taxation. We have heard the minister defend this feature of his loan, but I am free to confess his defense does not appeal to me. In my opinion, the terms were entirely unwarranted and uncalled for, and the bonds were handled most extravagantly and expensively. Long before this issue pi $700,000,000 was placed on the market, men of financial standing in the country and, indeed, the press, pointed out to the minister that what has happened would happen, namely, that the bonds would pass from the hands of the small holders into the hands of the large holders and these very men who have made their money out of the war, the war profiteers if you will, would be relieved by the purchase of these bonds from their just share of taxation. The minister stated that a bond free of income tax gave a better result than a taxable bond, advancing the reason that if the bonds were not tax free, the Government would have to pay a higher rate upon them and the amount of that interest would be much more than the amount we would receive by way of income tax. I am sure the minister will not tell this House that there was any occasion under any circumstances to pay a higher rate of interest for money than 5i per cent. Surely the minister will not say that Canadians do not think as much of their securities as they do of the securities of Greece or Roumania, and it was only the other day we had a statement in this House, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), that the rate of interest charged to Greece and Roumania was 5i per cent. To arrive at the amount of income we would receive from an income tax bond in this country, would necessitate in every case a calculation-we should have to know who held the bond, what the amount of the holdings were and -what his income tax and surtax would be, before we could arrive at any definite conclusion as to the amount we would receive-and I am sure the minister will not tell me or anybody else that .such a calculation has been made. I attended many of the meetings at which. these bonds were offered for sale, and the questions of tax free bonds or rates of interest were never discussed. The appeal was made to the people to buy the bonds, because our men were overseas and the Government needed money to finance them as regards food, clothing and munitions of war, and money to bring them home when opportunity offered. Nobody talked about income tax 223
bonds or rates of interest. It may be, and undoubtedly is, true that some of the larger dealers bought these bonds simply as a financial proposition. When they got to that point, the minister should have dealt with them strictly on a business basis, and the amount of bonds these men were permitted to take should have been restricted and two classes of bonds should have been issued, one income tax free, the other taxable and the taxable bond should have borne a higher rate of interest than the tax free bond, and, the Government should have had the privilege of retiring these tax-free bonds at will before maturity. This year the United States' Government issued a four-year loan with the privilege to the Government of retiring it in three years. They had two classes of bonds, one taxable bearing a rate of interest of 4j per cent and the other tax-exempt, bearing interest at the rate of 3| per cent. The Secretary of the Treasury at Washington made the calculation that oil a three-year bond the difference of the rate of interest between one that was tax free and one that was taxable, was one per cent. This Government, however, issues bonds at the maximum rate of interest of 6i per cent and for five, ten or fifteen years, without retiring privileges and yet we speak about how much credit is due to us for our financing.
I would call the attention of the House to the references made by the minister to the fact that our bonds have been readily selling during a time of stress and trouble and that to-day they are being sold at a premium. The reason for intimating this is that the people of this country have confidence in its securities.
While he did not say so, we gathered the impression from his remarks there was just a little credit due the Government for their method of financing. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman that they	are	entitled	to any	credit
for the issue of those Victory Loans on the terms on which they were issued. As a matter of fact, those bonds are selling at a premium to-day, not on account of the security but because the Government issued them under the market rate, and it did not take long for business men and the moneyed interests of the country to realize the fact. That is the reason they are selling at a premium. The millions of dollars that are going into the pockets of speculators today and that are being placed in the strong boxes of big financiers very properly belong to the treasury of the Dominion, and they are being placed in those strong boxes be-



cause the bonds-the best security of this country-were thrown absolutely upon the bargain counter. I am sure that when my hon. friend looks at the morning paper and sees 5i per cent bonds income tax free which were sold approximately six months ago, bonds that we paid brokers a commission for selling, bonds that we paid bankers a commission for handling, bonds that we paid newspapers thousands of dollars for advertising, and, in addition to that, gave 15 days interest as a bonus-when he sees these bonds selling at 106, he must ask himself, what does it mean? What rate of interest is the man receiving on his money who made that investment six months ago? He is receiving at the rate of 171 per cent per annum. Surely it must be apparent that we placed these bonds on the market under market value and that millions of the people's money have been given away through financial prodigality.
In reference to the principle of tax-free bonds, it has been argued from one end of the country to the other, and it has been discussed to more than some hon. gentlemen's liking, that it is undemocratic. Tax free bonds relieve the man who can best afford to pay his share of taxation and place the burden upon the man who can least stand it-the toiler, the wage-eainer or the small business man. That is one objection that the people have to tax-free bonds, and it is an objection which the hon. minister should take into considerat on.
These 51 per cent bonds really mean an investment of 7, 8 or 10 per cent for the men who have large incomes, if their income and surtax is taken into account, and the taxation they are relieved of must be borne by the rest of the people of the Dominion. I am sorry that the hon. minister said in answer to an inquiry the other day that he had not yet arrived at a definite conclusion as to the terms of the next proposed issue. Well, let me say to my hon. friend that the people of this country have reached a conclusion. No more tax-free bonds will be successfully issued if they have not back of them the good-will of the public. So far as 'I am personally concerned I say to the minister frankly that I cannot support any issue that makes no distinction in the rates of interest on bonds that are tax free and those that are not. In. the event of an issue similar in terms to the last, I shall certainly oppose it in my county. It may be that it does not matter very much how much we raise in the county of Essex, hut I can assure the hon. minister that when 
we get through the people will know what they are buying, and just who are escaping the burden of taxation and who are carrying it. I say that in all fairness, because it is an important matter and I am just as anxious as the hon. gentleman that any loan we put out shall be a success. But in order to be successful it must be based on fairness and equity and must appeal to the taxpayers of the country. It may occur to some hon. gentlemen opposite that there are plenty of big men in the country to take all the bonds even if the little fellows do not take them. If the issue is right the big men will take them; but my experience has been-as indeed has been that of most men of business-that the only man who is more afraid of losing his money than the million dollar man is the two million dollar man. The saying is trite but true, and I am not so sure that the big men will be quite ready to take the bonds if they realize that a strong and vigorous campaign will be inaugurated to eliminate by retroactive legislation any tax-free privileges granted subsequent to the armistice. I think, therefore, that it would be well for the minister to give this matter serious consideration.
Last year in the course of the debate on the Budget I suggested to the then Acting Minister of Finance that we should emulate if possible the example of the United States in the handling of these bonds. I pointed out that in the United States neither the bankers nor the brokers received compensation for their services, and I felt that we Canadians were just as patriotic and loyal as were the people in that country, and that under proper government leadership our people would respond, and the work could he done here on the same basis. It would appear to me, from the figures I have in my hand in connection with the loan that was placed last October, that this Government are still of the opinion that when it comes to money matters patriotic motives do not influence our people and that there must always be a commission and a rake-off. I have a statement here which shows that in connection with the 1918 Victory Loan we paid: Banks, ' $],356.000; advertising, $275,596.88; printing, $219,257.23; remuneration to brokers and bond firms-this is divided this year Into two classes, one called remuneration to brokers, and bond firms, $709,468.18, and the other, canvassers' commission, $2,250,000, making a total of $4,810,314.29. So that it cost us approximately $5,000,000 to sell our $700,000,000 worth of bonds, while the United States Government placed a loan

that realized over $6,000,000,000, the cost of which did not exceed one-tenth of one per cent, or less than $6,000,000. In the list of brokers who received compensation in connection with this loan it is interesting to observe names which somehow or other seem to have been much in evidence since the advent of Union Government. I see here our friends the Dominion Securities Corporation, with Mr. E. R. Wood as president, received for their services $48,995; I find our friends Messrs. Wood, Gundy & Company were paid $51,060, and A. E. Ames and Company $47,339. These gentlemen were said to be "commandeered" in this country. Well, let me point out to my hon. friend how such men are commandeered on the other side and what they do in Detroit, Michigan. I have here a letter from Mr. Norton, secretary of the Detroit Patriotic Fund, in which he gives me the facts as follows:
The total subscription to the fourth Liberty loan for Detroit and Wayne county was $80,-250;400. The total expense of the campaign was $ 2iS,3 lo. 7 4. The banks handled the bonds without charge and no commission was paid to the brokers.
In other words, in Michigan it cost 35 cents per thousand, while it costs us $7; or for every dollar they spent we spent $20. These are the facts in so far as that particular loan is concerned.	*
Might I be permitted to bring to the attention of the House something which comes a little more closely home, something that occurred on this side of the river. We have in Essex county five municipalities, which, in matters of this kind, always work in unison-Ojibway, Sandwich, Ford, Walker-ville and Windsor. When this matter came up we had a meeting to discuss it. A gentleman came from Toronto to represent the Toronto brokers. He told us what they proposed doing and on what basis they proposed to do it. He said that all subscriptions of $10,000 and over would go to what was called the special committee and that all under $10,000 were to be credited to the local committees and that upon this amount so collected a commission of one-half of one per cent would be paid. Our men at the meeting told him that in so far as we were concerned, we were quite willing to help the loan all we could, and that there could be no question of personal remuneration. We were willing to give all of our time without any personal remuneration. We organized, we were given our quota of $4,000,000, and we raised in these five municipalities over $7,500,000. The local teams were credited with $3,700,000 and the teams which were
223i
under the direction of the private brokers were credited with $4,000,000. In so far as the Toronto brokers are concerned, I do not know what remuneration, if any, they had in connection with this loan, but what 1 do know is that they had not anything more to do with it than the Montreal brokers or anybody else, because all they did was to have a man in our office in Windsor telephone to Toronto nightly the names of the " special " subscribers and the amounts subscribed. When this transaction was closed up we were sent a cheque by the Toronto brokers, I assume for our share of the commission, and that cheque amounted to $18,549. We deducted from that cheque all the expenses in connection with the campaign and in the expenses we included an item of $1,800 for advertising. The total expenses of our organization amounted to $5,400. We had $13,000 left and this we divided between the local G.W.V.A. and the Sportsman's Patriotic Society. That is just what a few of us did. If in a few municipalities like ours there could be a saving of $13,000 on subscriptions amounting approximately to $7,500,000, it is simple mathematical calculation to ascertain what could have been saved throughout Canada if a proper appeal had been made to the people along that line.
I have already said that we paid to the banks the sum of $1,356,000 for their services in handling the bonds, and I have quoted in contrast the facts with regard to Detroit. I say that it is to the eternal discredit of the banks of this country that they should have exacted that sum from the people of Canada. When one considers the prosperity of the banks during the period since the war began, when one realizes that their profits have been so great from year to year that, in fact, within the last year there has, to use the parlance of the street, been some "melon cutting" amongst them, and that they have issued new stock at 30, 40 and 60 points under the market, one can see how little justification the banks had for the course which they pursued in connection with the Victory Loan. Surely the banks should have been willing to do what the banks on the other side, great and small, have been doing; that is, give their services to the country without being compensated for every single thing they did. The Minister of Finance has been paying 51 per cent for his money and we are told that money is dear and that it is going to be dearer. In fact, everything has gone up. Everybody is complaining about the

high cost of living. But we do not hear any one saying anything about the rate of interest allowed to depositors going up; it is just the same as it	was-three
per cent. That is a matter that the Government might investigate, particularly when it finds the hankers exacting from the people the last dollar. If the bankers insist upon having their pound of flesh, they should be made to pay the people a reasonable rate of interest on the money of the people that they are handling.
I want to say to my hon. friend in connection with this new loan that it is a most important thing, in my opinion, that the Government should have the support and good will of every person in this country, if.it is to get the best results. The Government have spent millions of dollars, but now they are up against the court of final appeal. They have to go to the people for money. When they do that they had better satisfy the people that they are going to give them a square deal, and the people are not satisfied that they are getting that in connection with the income tax free bond.
There is another matter that I should like to take up, a question that has been dealt with before in this House. I refer to bank amalgamations. The matter was pretty fairly discussed here some weeks ago and it seemed to be the consensus of opinion amongst hon. members that we have had enough bank amalgamations for some time in Canada. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) told us that while ten years ago there were thirty banks in Canada, to-day there are sixteen. I think he likewise told us that at that time there were deposits of $800,000,000 while to-day there are deposits of $1,600,000,000 or one-half as many banks and twice as much money on deposit. The result of these amalgamations is to place in the hands of a few men the control of the financial resources of the country. It works out to the detriment of the small communities. It is making money centres out of one or two of the principal cities, which is not a good thing for the country. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance in dealing with bank amalgamations the other night,-and I was very much impressed with his remarks-said that there were four parties to be considered in connection with a bank amalgamation. First there are the depositors, second the shareholders, third the borrowers, and then the general public. Well, Sir, I have yet to learn in any bank amalgamation that has

taken place in this country where the depositors have been consulted. They have nothing whatever to say. The amalgamations go into effect and the money of the depositors follows, as a matter of course. Now, it would not be a bad idea if the bankers of this country realized that, after all, their holdings, in comparison with the moneys of the depositors, are rather small in the chartered banks of this country; they are simply the trustees of the people and not the absolute owners of the money that is there on deposit. To-day there is in paid-up capital in the banks of Canada, and likewise in the reserve funds-because we want to give the shareholders credit for everything *-approximately $230,000,000, whereas the deposits amount to $1,600,000,000. What does that mean? It means that for every dollar the shareholders have invested in the banks the public have seven. And yet the latter are not consulted in connection with amalgamations. So far as the depositors are concerned, they get the same old three per cent interest, whereas the shareholders get fat dividends and run the bank to suit themselves. Now the time has come in the interests of the Canadian public when, in dealing with the banks, more consideration should he given to the building up of the country by the Government. Our banks have much to recommend them, but in so far as the depositors and the small business men are concerned, in my opinion they are an expensive luxury. I would say, , in this connection, that it would be a good thing if the Government would investigate and take into consideration the advisability of opening a number of smaller banks, somewdiat on the line of the State banks in the country to the south. I have in my hand the report of the Bank Commissioner of the State of Massachusetts for the year 1917. It shows that they have in the state of Massachusetts 195 small savings banks with deposits to the amount of $1,250,000,000, which is within $350,000,000 of what we have in the banks of the whole of Canada. What do we find further? There they have no shareholders in the banks. The depositors are the shareholders, under Government supervision. They get credit for the interest earned on the money, and they are charged with the expense of handling it.
I have already said that in Canada the depositors obtain three per cent on their money, whereas the banks, and I think I am not doing them any injustice when I say so, obtain an average rate of interest on that money of six per cent, or a spread equal to the rate of interest paid. Now what do we find in the case of the banks iri Mas-

saehusetts? I have the reports and they show that for the year mentioned the banks charge for the use of money to customers interest at 4.88 per cent, and the average rate of interest they allow to the depositor for his money is 4.05 per cent, a spread of less than	one-third of one
per cent.	That	is the	reason
I say that our system is too expensive, and the Government should seriously consider, in the interests of small banks and of depositors, the advisability of introducing some changes in the system in order that more of a parity should be maintained and there should not be such a spread between the cost of handling money and the expense of borrowing it.
There is another matter I would touch upon for a minute, which concerns the people of this country, and that is bank premises. We all know that from Halifax to Vancouver the Canadian banks ordinarily have very ornate, handsome, and expensive premises. I think we are safe in estimating that one-half of the paid-up capital of the banks in this country is invested in office buildings. I believe there should he some government supervision and some restriction on the amount the banks can invest in office buildings not only in this country but abroad. I saw in a New York paper not very long ago where one of the Canadian banks had paid over $1,000,000 for office buildings in New York city. That money is locked up when it is needed to develop the industrial and the agricultural life of the country. In my opinion the Government should see that the bankers are kept under some restriction in that regard. There is no reason why the Government should not give serious attention to this and other subjects, and endeavour to ascertain if we cannot do something more than we are doing for the people of this country.
It is rather late in the day to my mind, but a committee has been appointed to investigate the high cost of living. I have the greatest respect for the members of that Committee, and I do hope that they will accomplish something, but I have my doubts. Personally, I believe the matter is largely in the hands of the Government. They must expect that where there has been the lavish issue of paper money and bonds that has taken place in this country-where issues have been made by the hale-the cost of living is going to be high. That is the history of every country under similar conditions. In addition to that, I would like to point out a reason that appeals to me as being one why the cost of living increases
and continues to soar, and that is in connection with the advances recently made for credits to countries across the seas. There is not a wholesaler or a retailer in Canada whose shelves are filled, they are all practically empty, and yet we have the Government of the day going out and borrowing the money of the people to finance manufacturers to sell abroad necessaries at war prices. They ask our people on the one hand to finance these undertakings for them and on the other hand they ask them to go and purchase for home consumption these very same goods at the prices so established. Is it any wonder that prices continue to soar? It is unreasonable to expect them to remain where they are. My own thought is that if the Government would simply stop this financial merry-go-round and permit trade and commerce to take its natural channel without being artificially supported by Government credits, we would get back to normal conditions and down to a reasonable basis of living. As I see it, Mr. Speaker, what we have to do in this country is to look the situation clearly in the face. There is no use in putting off the evil day. We are a country of but eight imillions of people, we owe $2,900,000,000, and it is going to take $300,000,000 to carry us over this year. These are the conditions and the facts that have to be faced. But with it all we have a country of wonderful natural resources, we have a people who are courageous and have confidence in themselves and in their country, and if this Government will only give us sane financial legislation then I believe we will work out our salvation.
Mr. JAMES Me IS A A.C (King's, P.E.I.): Mr. Speaker-
In view of the lateness of the hour, will the hon. gentleman move the adjournment of the debate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman had better proceed.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is the most important that comes before Parliament at any time, and at no time, we may take it for granted, has the importance of the Budget been as great as on the present occasion, for the reason that it is a war Budget. We are yet at war. It is true that the fighting has ceased-for the time being at least-but the terms of peace have not been signed, peace has not been officially proclaimed.' And more than that, our troops have not all been demobilized. The conse-

quence is that a very large amount of money will be required for demobilization and other matters in connection with the war. Having this in view, it is our business to seriously take into account how best the necessary money can be obtained, and this brings up at once the question of our fiscal policy.
In this connection it would be a waste of time to discuss theoretical policies-free trade, protection, moderate protection, lower tariff, and so on. These would be simply shibboleths. The all-important question is the policy which is best adapted to the conditions of our country at this particular time, and which will afford, according to our traditions, the easiest and surest way of raising the money necessary to carry on the affairs of the nation.
In the first place, Sir, if we take into account, as has been more than once brought before the House during this debate, our position relative to the protective countries of the world, and especially our position with regard to our neighbour to the south- a highly protected country which has brought its fiscal policy to such a degree of perfection that its industries have been brought to their highest state of development-we see that were Canada to depart from her protective policy she would be at the mercy of this great and powerful neighbour, and it appears to me that it would be very difficult for us to retain even tfiose industries which we have succeeded in bringing to a certain degree of development, and, in some cases, to the very highest perfection.
The hon. member speaks of protection. Is he in favour of protected potatoes or free potatoes for Prince n*dward Island?

Potatoes are free. Mr. Speaker, not only is this, to which I have referred, the best fiscal policy for this country, but it is the fiscal policy under which we have carried on our public business for forty years-during almost the whole history of this confedterated Dominion the fiscal policy has been that of protection. And in the change of government, notwithstanding the professions that were made prior to 1896 by our friends opposite that protection should be pulled out root and branch, and the maledictions they hurled against this fiscal policy, as I frequently heard myself, yet when they assumed power and during all the years that they remained in power they
11 p.m. carried on the business of the country under practically the

same fiscal policy as that which was inaugurated by Sir John A. Macdonald when he initiated the National Policy. It is true, there have been some minor changes here and there in the way of readjustments, but they were infinitesimal. And that is the same policy that has prevailed from that time down to the present session,-the policy prevailing under the (Laurier tariff of 1907. So that when we are told by our friends on t'he Opposition side that a new era must now be brought about,. and that protection must not be any longer the policy of this country, surely they can have not the slightest hope that they will be able to persuade the members of this House or the people of this country to take them seriously.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of these facts it is our duty to stand by that which will afford the Government the best and surest means of securing the money necessary to meet our great obligations. We have been told by the Finance Minister of the amount of our national debt, of the various expenditures for this year, of the interest on the public debt, and of the pensions- all which involve immense sums of money; then the revenue is summed up, and we find there will be quite a difference between the revenue and the expenditure. We shall have, according to the figures presented to us by the Finance Minister, a total revenue of $280,000,000, the ordinary expenditure will be $270,000,000, the capital expenditure, $50,000,000, and in addition there will be an estimated expenditure for war purposes of $300,000,000. That is quite a formidable array of figures. The Government has to grapple with this problem and find some means of meeting these obligations. But is this the time for us to depart from the fiscal policy followed by Governments of this country for forty years? Is this an opportune time for us to lop off that portion of the revenue which is derived from the customs tariff- $145,000,000 estimated for the present fiscal year -and make a plunge into unknown and hitherto untried methods of raising money to meet the public expenditure? Is this the time to adopt unproven and uncertain methods which are likely to prove ruinous to the country? Is this the time to make such a departure?
There are a number of other matters to which I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, but I hardly feel equal to the occasion tonight. I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

On the motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11.07 p.m.
Tuesday, June 17, 1919.
